entry.title: Erotapokriseis XII
entry.content:
EN:

Hello, my dear readers,

I’ve responded to most of your emails, but I thought I would answer a few of your questions here as well. And first, thank you so much for reading and for all your thoughtful feedback. It really means a lot to me! :) I have news!

As some of you wanted, I migrated the blog to Substack a few weeks ago. Some of you kept telling me, “Filiz, we check your page from time to time to see if you posted something. Is there some way to know when you publish?” Apparently, yes! :D If you leave your email address on Substack, I think it lets you know whenever I publish something. So this is our third migration now. :) First Medium, then GitHub, and now Substack.

But! We are not actually leaving GitHub. I will still post everything here, and it will also appear on Substack. Substack is basically just there to tell you, “Hey, Filiz posted something.” :D Also, Substack is not really a good place for my science posts anyway because it cannot properly render equations, so for those posts, I will probably just put a small paragraph there and direct you here for the actual article. Ay, I wrote so much just to explain this. :D

Basically: WE ARE STILL ON GITHUB! And, and, aaaand… this took some courage, but I opened the anonymous question box again. :D You can now write to me anonymously under every post. I just hope we do not return to the same gossip-y, absurd questions from before. Please behave. :D For now, the anonymous box will stay open under each post, and you can ask me whatever you would like there.

And really, thank you so much.

Thanks for reading. :)

TR:

Merhaba sevgili okurlarım :)

Çoğunuzun maillerine cevap verdim ama birkaç şeyi buradan da söyleyeyim istedim. Öncelikle okuduğunuz, yazdığınız ve güzel geri dönüşleriniz için çok teşekkür ederim! Küçük bir haberim de var: Birkaç hafta önce, isteyenler olduğu için blogu Substack’e de taşıdım. Ama merak etmeyin, hâlâ GitHub’dayız! :) Yazılarımı yine burada yayınlayacağım; Substack daha çok yeni bir şey yazdığımda size haber versin diye var. Zaten bilim yazıları için pek uygun değil, denklemleri düzgün render edemiyor. Bir de biraz cesaretimi toplayıp anonim soru kutusunu yeniden açtım; şimdilik her yazının altında bana anonim olarak yazabilirsiniz. Umarım bu kez önceki gibi magazinsel ve absürt sorular gelmez. :) Ve tekrar, gerçekten çok teşekkür ederim. :)

1) Q: Does the apparent fine-tuning of the universe (The Fine-Tuned Universe) fill you with wonder, or with suspicion? And, If the constants of the universe could have been otherwise, does that weaken our idea of reality?

A: Suspicion, mostly. In physics, whenever a number looks suspiciously tuned, it often means we are missing the deeper theory that makes it inevitable, not that someone set a dial. Wonder at the universe always; but “fine-tuned” is usually nature telling me my equations aren’t finished yet. :)

And for the second question: Not really, because we don’t actually know they could have been otherwise. We have no complete theory of where the constants come from, and ignorance isn’t the same as contingency. Reality isn’t weakened by our not reaching the bottom; it’s just still holding something back.

2) Q: If we are constantly changing (The Problem of the Self), in what sense are we still the same person?

A: In no fixed sense, and I’ve made peace with that. There’s no little core “me” sitting untouched beneath the changes, only a continuity, a thread of memory and pattern that keeps re-tying itself. I’m not the same person. I’m the same story, still being told.

I don’t think being the same person requires remaining the same thing. The child I was, the person I was ten years ago, and the person writing this now would disagree about an astonishing number of things. Some of my fears disappeared, some convictions became stronger, others I abandoned completely. Even many of my memories have probably changed in the remembering. If identity depended on preserving some fixed set of traits, I would have stopped being “me” many times already. What persists is not a substance but a relationship between these different versions. I remember being her. I inherited consequences from her decisions. Some of her loves, wounds, habits, questions, and promises reached me, even when their form changed along the way. And whatever I do now will become part of the person I am later, even if she eventually looks back at me with the same mixture of affection and disbelief with which I look at my younger selves.

So I think sameness is closer to continuity than identity. A river is still called by the same name even though none of its water stays put. Maybe we are something like that. Not because there is an invisible essence holding everything together, but because one state flows into another without a clean break. This is also why I don’t feel particularly threatened by the idea that there is no permanent self. I actually find it comforting. It means I don’t owe lifelong loyalty to every version of myself I have ever been. I can outgrow beliefs, revise myself, become softer in some places and harder in others, and none of that is a betrayal of some “true” Filiz hidden underneath. There may be no final version underneath. So again: I’m not the same person. I’m the same story, still being told. And perhaps even “the same story” is slightly too neat. Stories get edited too. :)

3) Q: When scale changes (The Renormalization Group), do only the equations change, or does the language of reality change too?

A: Both, and that is the deep part. The couplings run with scale, yes, but so does the vocabulary of what we are willing to call fundamental. Quarks and gluons give way to protons, protons to nuclei, and yesterday’s ontology quietly becomes today’s microscopic detail. Renormalization is not merely the statement that our equations depend on scale. It is the rather inconvenient fact that nature seems under no obligation to preserve our favorite description of it. Reality speaks a different dialect at every scale, and reductionism does not get to declare one of them the only honest one!

4) Q: Do you find Faust understandable? At what point does the desire to know more become something tragic?

A: Completely understandable; the wanting-to-know is the least alien thing in the world to me. It turns tragic the moment knowing becomes a way of not living, when you would trade every actual morning for one more secret. Faust’s sin isn’t curiosity. It’s contempt for the ordinary hours.

He wants the universe to reveal itself to him, but he has no patience for the life already happening in front of him. At some point, the hunger to know everything becomes an inability to love anything that is merely finite.

Aren’t we all a little Faustian, though?

I recognize that impulse more than I would like to admit. I spent a long part of my life like a racehorse, and sometimes I still become one. There are moments when I have to stop and ask myself very simple questions: Why am I rushing? What am I actually feeling? What is already good here? Sometimes you can still be hungry for more and say, quite deliberately, enough for now.

Perhaps this is also why I have grown suspicious of the modern obsession with “leaving your comfort zone.” Apparently every quiet corner of life must now be escaped, optimized, or turned into personal growth. I don’t believe that. Temperance matters. Knowing when to pursue more is important, but knowing when to tell your own appetite to be quiet is a kind of wisdom too. A little grandmotherly, perhaps, but grandmothers have occasionally been right about things.

5) Q: As someone who plays Go, do you think the game reveals a person’s intelligence more, or their character?

A: Character, without question!

Intelligence may get you through the opening, but the middlegame tells me much more about you: how you behave when you are losing, whether you become greedy when you are ahead, whether you panic inside a messy position, whether you can stay patient when the board refuses to go the way you planned. Over a full game, it becomes very difficult to hide yourself. The stones keep a surprisingly honest record.

There is also one quality I have noticed in almost every Go player I consider truly good: temperance. They are usually humble, patient, and very difficult to provoke. And you can learn quite a lot about a person simply from how much space they are willing to leave you. Some players want everything. Every corner, every side, every little point. Others seem to understand instinctively that a good game needs room for two people.

And this may sound strange, but after playing people from many different places, I sometimes feel as though I can glimpse little cultural habits on the board too. Please read this as cultural codes, not stereotypes! These are only my own impressions from the people I have happened to play.

When I play Americans, for example, I often feel as if we are not exactly playing together. It feels more like two people independently building their own games on the same board.

Turkish players feel much more emotional to me. Even when you attack them, they sometimes hesitate before attacking back, almost as if they are thinking, “Maybe she does not really mean it as an attack.” :D There is a strange amount of emotional interpretation happening between the stones.

With French players, I always feel as if we are flirting with the game. One move forward, one move back, approach, retreat, approach again… and for some reason nobody wants to finish anything. Ahahah.

Japanese players, at least the ones I have played, tend to approach the board very harmoniously. There is almost an aesthetic responsibility attached to every stone. The game should not only work, it should somehow look right. Very reserved, almost as if winning is not terribly important to them, while every tiny move is, of course, quietly helping them win.

Chinese players have usually been the hardest for me. They can be incredibly calm. Quiet, patient, almost unreadable. Nothing dramatic happens, nothing looks particularly threatening, and meanwhile they are absolutely trying to kill you. :D Playing them sometimes gives me the feeling of saman altından su yürütmek: everything looks peaceful on the surface while something very serious is happening underneath.

And since I am happily analyzing everyone else, I should probably say how I play too.

I usually begin with very good composure. Calm, patient, sensible Filiz. :D But I am also affected by the person across from me, so at some point I tend to become emotionally involved in the game. Then I have to catch myself, put the emotion aside, and return to what I actually enjoy most, which is not simply defeating the other person but building something interesting with them on the board.

My calmness and patience are often misunderstood, though. Apparently this is not limited to real life; I am misunderstood in Go too. Eh, I am used to it by now. :)

What I find funny is that by the end of the game, my opponent is often annoyed with me, sometimes even a little upset. They tend to underestimate the small things I build on the board. They look too minor, too local, too insignificant to have any real effect, so they do not take them very seriously.

I never really mind being underestimated. :)

Because sometimes that little thing they dismissed for half the game turns out to be the stone that kills them!

6) Q: Does symmetry breaking feel to you like the loss of order, or like the emergence of reality? And if perfect symmetry is only an unseen possibility, is the world we live in real precisely because it is imperfect?

A: Emergence, every time. The symmetry is still there in the laws; the world simply has to pick one concrete solution in order to exist, and in the picking, structure appears: direction, mass, a magnet’s north. Order is not lost when symmetry breaks. That is the exact moment a featureless possibility becomes a real thing.

And to answer your second question, yes, and I find that almost tender. Perfect symmetry is sameness in every direction, which is another way of saying nothing has happened yet. It is potential, not existence! Ah! :) The world we live in is the broken one, and the breaking is precisely what allowed anything to take shape at all. Perhaps imperfection is not what went wrong with reality. Perhaps it is what made reality possible in the first place!

7) Q: Did the idea that gravity is not a force but the geometry of spacetime (General Relativity) change your intuition about reality? What moves you most about it: its mathematical beauty, or the way it almost turns the world inside out?

A: Profoundly! The turning-inside-out, though the beauty is how it does it. Once you absorb that a planet orbiting the sun is just following the straightest line it can through curved spacetime, “force” stops being fundamental and becomes a story we told before we saw the shape of things. Nothing pulls the Earth; it goes straight, and the straight is bent.

That is what moves me most about general relativity: Einstein didn’t add a force; he changed what space and time are. The radical move was not to complicate reality, but to see it differently. It’s the rare case where the more radical idea is also the more elegant one, and reality sided with the radical.

This question came in Turkish.

8) Q: Sizi uzaktan okuyan birinin hakkınızda yanılacağı en tehlikeli şey ne olurdu?

A: Beni yalnızca aklımdan ibaret sanması.

Blogda daha çok düşünen tarafım görünüyor tabii. Fizik, felsefe, kitaplar, kavramlar, biraz itiraz, biraz merak, biraz da “bir dakika ama burada bir sorun var” hali. :) O yüzden beni sadece ciddi, soğuk, fazla entelektüel ya da ulaşılması zor biri gibi hayal etmek kolay olabilir.

Ama ben yalnızca düşünen biri değilim. Çok gülen, çok seven, sevdiği insanlara karşı fazlasıyla yumuşayan, bazen çocuk gibi heyecanlanan, bazen de çok basit şeylerle mutlu olan biriyim. Güzel bir yemek, deniz kenarı, sevdiğim birinin sesi, iyi yazan bir kalem, beklenmedik bir nezaket, küçük bir şaka… Bunlar beni sandığınızdan daha kolay yakalar.

Belki de hakkımda en yanlış anlaşılabilecek şey şu: Derinlik ile sertliği aynı şey sanmak. Ben derinliği severim, ama sertliği sevmem. Zekâyı severim, ama gösterişini değil. Gücü severim, ama kabalığını değil.

Beni gerçekten tanımak isteyen biri, ne düşündüğüme baktığı kadar, neye inceldiğime de bakmalı bence. İnsan kendini yalnızca fikirlerinde değil, yumuşadığı yerlerde de ele verir.

This question came in Turkish.

9) Q: MR yazınız kalbime çok dokundu. Kendimize mutluluk borcumuz var hakikaten. Şimdi nasılsınız? İyileştiniz mi?

A: Ah, ne mutlu bana duygularim yaziyi okuyana gecebildiyse… Tesekkur ederim. Daha iyiyim. Her gun iyi olmaya calisiyorum. Calisiyorum, yeni seyler ogreniyorum, geziyorum, haftasonlarimi dolu dolu geciriyorum. Sevdigim yemekleri yiyorum. Daha da iyi olacagim. Daha mutlu olmak istiyorum. Vucudumu iyilestirmeye calisiyorum. Iyilesecegim. :)

This question came in Turkish.

10) Q: Sizi seven insanların sizde gördüğü ama sizin kendinizde görmekte zorlandığınız şey ne?

A: Belki de ne kadar sevilebilir olduğumu.

Bunu yazmak bile biraz garip hissettiriyor. :) Ama sanırım doğru cevap bu. Beni seven insanlar bende sıcaklık, sadakat, komiklik, inatçılık, zeka, bazen de çocuk gibi bir heyecan gördüklerini söylüyorlar. Ben ise çoğu zaman kendimi eksiklerimden, yetişemediklerimden, yapamadıklarımdan ibaret görmeye daha yakınım. Hatta bazen hakettiğimden fazla sevildiğimi bile düşünüyorum.

Sevildiğinizde insan biraz şaşırıyor. Çünkü siz kendinizi içeriden biliyorsunuz; dağınıklığınızı, korkularınızı, beceremediğiniz şeyleri, geç kaldığınız yerleri. Ama başkaları bazen sizin kendinizden sakladığınız iyi tarafları daha net görüyor.

Sanırım bu yüzden sevilmek benim için aynaya bakmak gibi değil. Bir yerde öyle olması gerektiğini okumuştum. Benim için daha çok, benim göremediğim bir pencerenin açılması gibi sevilmek.

This is not a question.

11) C: I loved your piece on Wittgenstein—absolutely loved it. Though actually, “loved” might not be quite the right word. I was so triggered by it that I stopped reading two or three times. But I kept going back to it, thinking, okay, what the hell is she actually getting at? Eventually I made it to the end, and then, more or less at random, read your “I Do Not Want to Be Silent” section. And you reminded me exactly why I have such a visceral dislike of academic philosophy. I remember thinking, damn, this woman’s got balls. There’s such clarity in the way you think. I’m really glad I stumbled across your blog.

A: Thank you, this made me laugh. :) Honestly, the fact that you stopped reading two or three times, got annoyed, and still came back to ask yourself what the hell I was trying to say might be one of the nicest compliments you could give me!

And “damn, this woman’s got balls” absolutely made my day. Ahahah. :)

I think part of my problem with academic philosophy is that it can become so dry, sterile, and insulated that it starts to feel like a comfortable little world for people who do not particularly want to be disturbed.

I am really glad you found the blog. And even more glad you kept reading after wanting to throw Wittgenstein at the wall. :))

Also, since you wrote anonymously, I have no way of reaching you. If you are ever in Dallas or somewhere nearby, please write to me. I would genuinely love to have coffee with you.

Much love, Filiz

11) C: If I could step inside your mind like a private museum, what would be waiting for me in the very first room?

A: That’s such an interesting question. Thank you for asking!

I don’t know. Probably not a very tidy place. :)

There would probably be half-finished books on the table, papers with notes on them, fountain pens, silly little objects, maybe one or two pieces of origami. And somewhere, definitely, there would be the sea. Because no matter how much I live in Dallas now, a part of my mind still feels like it stayed in İzmir, maybe even a little in Urla.

I don’t think there would be any grand answers in the first room. More like small things. A feeling left from the books I read as a child, the smell of the sea, the sounds of my grandmother moving around in the kitchen, and sometimes, the smell of freshly baked cake waiting for me when I came home tired from playing outside. Things I have tried to understand but still haven’t fully understood, underlined sentences I was probably too young to understand but somehow refused to leave behind, unfinished notebooks, questions I sometimes take too seriously, and maybe a little embarrassment about how intensely I have always cared about things that other people seemed able to pass by so easily.

My mind keeps evidence of attempts, not only achievements. There would probably be some physics in one corner too. I won’t say a blackboard, that would be too dramatic, but yes, some equations, some concepts, some “wait, but why is it like this?” moments. :)

I think the person leaving that room would understand this about me: I am not someone who has finished most things. I am more someone who keeps returning to certain things. Some things are not there because they were left unfinished. Some things are there because they are still alive in me.

I am always in metaxy. As long as I live, I think I will remain somewhere in that in-between. I made peace with that feeling a long time ago.

entry.title: Entropy and the Arrow of Time — Why You Cannot Unscramble an Egg

link.title: Entropy and the Arrow of Time — Why You Cannot Unscramble an Egg

entry.content:
Every fundamental law of physics is time-symmetric!

Newton’s equations: time-symmetric!

Maxwell’s equations: time-symmetric!

Schrödinger’s equation: time-symmetric!

Even the Standard Model is time-symmetric (with one tiny, almost negligible exception)!

Run the equations forward!

Run them backward!

They don’t care. ( DO NOT CARE! )

And yet — you have never seen a shattered glass reassemble itself.

You have never seen smoke pour back into a cigarette.

You have never seen a scrambled egg unscramble.

There is a direction to time. An arrow. And only one law in physics knows about it.

The Second Law of Thermodynamics!

What Entropy Actually Is

The intuitive definition — “entropy is disorder” — is not wrong, but it is dangerously imprecise!

The correct definition is due to Boltzmann (1877):

\[S = k_B \ln \Omega\]

where \(\Omega\) is the number of microstates compatible with a given macrostate, and \(k_B\) is Boltzmann’s constant.

A macrostate is what you can observe — temperature, pressure, volume. A microstate is the exact position and momentum of every particle.

An intact egg corresponds to a small number of microstates — the proteins must be arranged just so, the yolk here, the white there. A scrambled egg corresponds to an astronomically larger number of microstates — almost any arrangement of denatured proteins looks scrambled.

The Second Law, in Boltzmann’s language:

Systems evolve toward macrostates with more microstates because there are simply more ways to be there.

This is not a force. Not a field. Not an interaction. It is pure combinatorics applied to an absurdly large number of particles.

The Boltzmann H-Theorem and Its Paradox

In 1872, Boltzmann proved the H-theorem: for a gas of particles evolving under classical mechanics, a certain quantity H decreases monotonically over time. \(-H\) is essentially entropy. So entropy increases. QED.

Except — there was a problem.

Loschmidt’s reversibility paradox (1876): If every microscopic collision is time-reversible, how can the macroscopic evolution be irreversible? For every trajectory where entropy increases, there exists a time-reversed trajectory where entropy decreases.

Boltzmann’s answer was essentially statistical: entropy-decreasing trajectories exist but are so astronomically rare that you will never observe one.

The universe, at the Big Bang, started in an extraordinarily low-entropy state. It has been evolving toward higher entropy ever since. The arrow of time is not written into the laws of physics — it is written into the initial conditions of the universe.

This is sometimes called the Past Hypothesis (David Albert, 2000): the universe began in an extremely special, low-entropy macrostate.

Why? We don’t know. This is one of the deepest open questions in physics.

Entropy and Information

In 1948, Claude Shannon — working on communication theory — defined the entropy of a probability distribution:

\[H = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i\]

This is formally identical to Boltzmann’s entropy. Not approximately. Exactly, up to constants.

This is not a coincidence.

Information and entropy are the same thing, viewed from different angles.

When you learn the microstate of a system, its entropy — from your perspective — decreases. You have gained information. The system has lost entropy.

This connection was made precise by Maxwell’s Demon (1867) — a thought experiment where a tiny demon sorts fast and slow molecules, apparently decreasing entropy without doing work.

The resolution, due to Szilard (1929) and Landauer (1961): the demon must store information about each molecule. When it erases that information — as it must, eventually — it dissipates heat into the environment.

Erasing one bit of information dissipates at least:

\[k_B T \ln 2 \text{ joules of heat}\]

This is Landauer’s principle — experimentally verified in 2012.

Information is physical. Computation has a thermodynamic cost. The demon cannot win.

Black Holes and the Entropy Bound

In 1972, Jacob Bekenstein proposed something radical:

Black holes have entropy.

Specifically, the entropy of a black hole is proportional to the area of its event horizon — not its volume:

\[S_{BH} = \frac{k_B c^3}{4 G \hbar} A = \frac{A}{4 l_P^2}\]

where \(l_P\) is the Planck length and \(A\) is the horizon area.

Hawking confirmed this by showing black holes emit thermal radiation — Hawking radiation — with a temperature:

\[T_H = \frac{\hbar c^3}{8 \pi G M k_B}\]

The Bekenstein-Hawking entropy is not a metaphor. It is the actual, physical entropy of a black hole.

This led to the holographic principle (t’Hooft, Susskind): the maximum entropy of any region of space is proportional to its boundary area, not its volume.

The universe may be, in some deep sense, a hologram — all the information needed to describe a volume of space encoded on its boundary surface.

The Heat Death of the Universe

The Second Law has a cosmological implication that is difficult to sit with.

The universe is evolving toward maximum entropy. Stars will burn out. Black holes will evaporate via Hawking radiation. Eventually — on timescales of \(10^{100}\) years and beyond — the universe will reach thermal equilibrium.

No temperature gradients. No free energy. No work possible. No life. No thought. No structure of any kind.

This is the heat death of the universe.

It is, as far as we know, inevitable.

Why This Is the Most Profound Law in Physics

The other laws of physics describe how things move. The Second Law describes why things happen at all.

Without entropy gradients — without the arrow of time — there is no causality, no memory, no narrative. You cannot remember the past because the past was lower entropy and the future is higher. The direction of time is the direction of entropy increase.

You are a low-entropy structure maintaining itself against the universal tendency toward disorder. :) Yeah, I think we can frame it like that!

Every thought you have, every computation your brain performs, dissipates heat into the environment — exactly as Landauer said!

Thinking has a thermodynamic cost! ( oo yeah! :) )

The universe is running down… We are, briefly, running against it…

That, I think, is enough! (Ahahahah, writing this line made me feel like I was narrating a documentary! Anyway, cheers!)

P.S. I’ll add the further reading and sources later. I’m kind of sick right now! Thank you for reading. :)

entry.title: The Planck Scale: Where Physics Ends and the Unknown Begins

link.title: The Planck Scale: Where Physics Ends and the Unknown Begins

entry.content:
There is a length scale at which everything we know stops working.

Not approximately stops working. Not becomes less accurate.

Stops working.

At the Planck length:

\[\ell_P = \sqrt{ rac{\hbar G}{c^3}} \approx 1.616 imes 10^{-35} ext{ m}\]

quantum mechanics and general relativity simultaneously produce nonsensical predictions.

Infinities appear that cannot be renormalized. Spacetime itself loses its smooth structure. The concept of “distance” becomes undefined. The causal structure of spacetime breaks down.

This is not a problem waiting to be solved by better mathematics.

It is the edge of the map.

Beyond it: here be dragons.

I. How the Planck Units Arise

In 1899, Max Planck noticed something remarkable.

The fundamental constants of nature:

\[\hbar = 1.055 imes 10^{-34} ext{ J·s} \quad ext{(quantum of action)}\] \[G = 6.674 imes 10^{-11} ext{ m}^3 ext{kg}^{-1} ext{s}^{-2} \quad ext{(gravitational constant)}\] \[c = 2.998 imes 10^8 ext{ m/s} \quad ext{(speed of light)}\]

These can be combined to form units of length, mass, time, and energy that involve no human conventions whatsoever.

The meter is defined by human choice. The kilogram is defined by human choice. The second is defined by human choice.

The Planck units are defined by nature.

\[\ell_P = \sqrt{ rac{\hbar G}{c^3}} \approx 1.616 imes 10^{-35} ext{ m}\] \[m_P = \sqrt{ rac{\hbar c}{G}} \approx 2.176 imes 10^{-8} ext{ kg}\] \[t_P = \sqrt{ rac{\hbar G}{c^5}} \approx 5.391 imes 10^{-44} ext{ s}\] \[E_P = m_P c^2 = \sqrt{ rac{\hbar c^5}{G}} \approx 1.956 imes 10^9 ext{ J} \approx 1.22 imes 10^{19} ext{ GeV}\]

These are the scales at which the three fundamental constants, $\hbar$ (quantum), $G$ (gravity), $c$ (relativity), all become simultaneously order unity.

At the Planck scale, quantum effects, gravitational effects, and relativistic effects are all equally important.

No theory we have can handle all three simultaneously.

II. Why Both Theories Break Down

General Relativity breaks down at the Planck scale because quantum fluctuations of the metric become order-unity.

In GR, spacetime is a smooth manifold: a differentiable geometric structure on which the metric tensor $g_{\mu u}$ is defined.

The Einstein equations:

\[G_{\mu u} = rac{8\pi G}{c^4} T_{\mu u}\]

relate the curvature of spacetime (left side) to the energy-momentum content (right side).

At the Planck scale, quantum fluctuations of the energy-momentum tensor, the zero-point fluctuations of all quantum fields, produce metric fluctuations of order unity:

\[\langle(\delta g_{\mu u})^2 angle \sim 1\]

The smooth manifold structure of spacetime breaks down. You cannot define distances. You cannot define causal structure. The tools of differential geometry, on which GR depends entirely, become inapplicable.

Quantum Field Theory breaks down at the Planck scale because it assumes a fixed, smooth spacetime background.

QFT is defined on a manifold. It uses the smooth structure of spacetime to define fields, propagators, Feynman diagrams.

When the manifold itself fluctuates quantum mechanically, when spacetime is no longer a fixed background but a dynamical quantum object, QFT has no foundation to stand on.

The standard renormalization procedure, absorbing UV divergences into physical parameters, fails when gravity is included.

Gravity is perturbatively non-renormalizable.

The coupling constant of gravity is:

\[ rac{E^2}{E_P^2}\]

At low energies $E \ll E_P$: small, still non-renormalizable but predictive as an effective field theory.

At the Planck scale $E \sim E_P$: order unity, infinitely many counterterms required, the theory loses all predictive power.

Both of our best theories fail simultaneously at the same scale. This is no coincidence. It is telling us something.

III. The Schwarzschild-Compton Coincidence

There is a beautiful argument for why the Planck scale is where things must break down.

Consider a particle of mass $m$.

The reduced Compton wavelength: The quantum mechanical scale below which the particle cannot be localized without pair production:

\[\lambda_C = rac{\hbar}{mc}\]

Below this scale, you cannot probe the particle without creating new particles. Quantum field theory is necessary.

The Schwarzschild radius: The gravitational scale at which the particle becomes a black hole:

\[r_S = rac{2Gm}{c^2}\]

Above this scale, the particle’s gravity prevents anything from escaping. General relativity is necessary.

Now ask: for what mass are these equal?

\[\lambda_C = r_S\] \[ rac{\hbar}{mc} = rac{2Gm}{c^2}\] \[m^2 = rac{\hbar c}{2G}\] \[m \sim m_P\]

At the Planck mass, the reduced Compton wavelength equals the Schwarzschild radius.

This means:

  • Below $m_P$: quantum effects dominate, gravity negligible
  • Above $m_P$: gravity dominates, $r_S > \lambda_C$, and confining the mass to its own quantum scale would make a black hole
  • At $m_P$: both are equally important, neither theory applies

The Planck mass is the mass at which quantum mechanics and gravity demand equal attention.

Neither can be ignored. Neither can handle the other.

IV. What Happens to Spacetime?

At the Planck scale, our concept of spacetime itself breaks down.

The Heisenberg uncertainty principle applied to gravity:

To measure a length $\delta x$, you need a probe with momentum:

\[\delta p \gtrsim rac{\hbar}{\delta x}\]

This probe has energy $E \sim \delta p \cdot c$ and therefore gravitational mass $m \sim E/c^2$.

This mass curves spacetime, creating a Schwarzschild radius:

\[r_S \sim rac{Gm}{c^2} \sim rac{G\hbar}{c^3 \delta x}\]

For the measurement to be meaningful, the probe must not collapse into a black hole:

\[\delta x \gtrsim r_S\] \[\delta x \gtrsim rac{G\hbar}{c^3 \delta x}\] \[(\delta x)^2 \gtrsim rac{G\hbar}{c^3} = \ell_P^2\] \[\delta x \gtrsim \ell_P\]

The Planck length is the minimum measurable length.

You cannot measure distances smaller than $\ell_P$. Not because of technological limitations. Because the act of measurement creates a black hole that destroys the information.

This suggests that spacetime is not continuous below the Planck scale.

The smooth manifold of GR, the infinite divisibility of space and time, is an approximation that breaks down at $\ell_P$.

What replaces it?

We don’t know.

V. The Planck Time and the Beginning

The Planck time:

\[t_P \approx 5.39 imes 10^{-44} ext{ s}\]

This is the time it takes light to travel one Planck length.

It is the shortest meaningful time interval.

The Big Bang occurred approximately $13.8 imes 10^9$ years ago.

In the standard cosmological model, we can extrapolate backward to $t \sim t_P$: one Planck time after the Big Bang.

Before that, at $t < t_P$, our physics breaks down.

We cannot describe what happened in the first Planck time after the Big Bang.

We cannot describe the Big Bang itself. We cannot describe what, if anything, preceded it.

The question “what happened before the Big Bang?” is not meaningless. It is simply unanswerable with current physics.

Not unanswerable in principle: perhaps a theory of quantum gravity will give us access to this regime.

But unanswerable with what we have.

The Planck time is the wall beyond which our knowledge cannot currently reach.

VI. The Planck Energy and Particle Physics

The Planck energy:

\[E_P \approx 1.22 imes 10^{19} ext{ GeV}\]

The LHC operates at:

\[E_{LHC} \approx 13.6 imes 10^3 ext{ GeV} = 1.36 imes 10^4 ext{ GeV}\]

The ratio:

\[ rac{E_P}{E_{LHC}} \approx 10^{15}\]

The LHC is fifteen orders of magnitude below the Planck energy.

To probe the Planck scale with a particle accelerator using current technology would require a machine the size of a galaxy.

This is no engineering challenge. It is a statement about the fundamental limits of direct experimental access to quantum gravity.

We will never build a Planck-scale accelerator.

This is one of the most profound constraints on empirical science.

The regime where quantum gravity operates, where our physics breaks down, is experimentally inaccessible by direct probing.

We must find indirect methods.

VII. Indirect Windows on the Planck Scale

Despite the inaccessibility of direct probing, there are several indirect windows on Planck-scale physics.

Cosmic rays:

Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory and the Telescope Array, reach energies up to $\sim 10^{20}$ eV = $10^{11}$ GeV.

Still eight orders of magnitude below the Planck energy. But the highest-energy particles we have access to.

Some quantum gravity models predict Lorentz invariance violation at high energies, modifications to the dispersion relation:

\[E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4 \pm \xi rac{E^3}{E_P}\]

A term like this shifts the thresholds of the reactions that shape the cosmic ray spectrum, above all the photopion production responsible for the GZK cutoff.

The observed spectrum matches the Lorentz-invariant prediction. Fitting the Auger data constrains the dimension-five coefficient to $\lvert\xi vert \lesssim 10^{-3}$.

No violation found. Yet.

Gamma-ray bursts:

GRBs are the most energetic events in the universe. Their photons travel cosmological distances.

If Lorentz invariance is violated at the Planck scale, if high-energy photons travel slightly faster than low-energy photons, simultaneous emission would arrive at different times.

The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope has constrained this with GRB 090510:

\[E_{QG,1} > 7.6 \, E_P\]

The energy at which linear Lorentz violation would become strong has been pushed above the Planck energy itself.

Models requiring $E_{QG,1} \lesssim E_P$ are disfavored.

Lorentz invariance holds to extraordinary precision.

The Cosmological Constant:

The vacuum energy density predicted by QFT:

\[ ho_{vacuum} \sim rac{E_P^4}{\hbar^3 c^3} \approx 10^{113} ext{ J/m}^3\]

The observed cosmological constant:

\[ ho_\Lambda \approx 10^{-9} ext{ J/m}^3\]

The discrepancy: 122 orders of magnitude.

This is the worst prediction in the history of physics.

It is directly related to the Planck scale, to the UV cutoff of quantum field theory.

The cosmological constant problem is a Planck-scale problem. Its resolution requires understanding what happens at the Planck scale.

We have no idea how to resolve it.

VIII. Approaches to Quantum Gravity

Given that we need a theory of quantum gravity, a theory that applies at the Planck scale, what are the serious candidates?

String Theory:

Replaces point particles with one-dimensional strings of length $\sim \ell_P$.

In string theory the minimum length is the string length $\ell_s$, which is related to but distinct from $\ell_P$.

String theory is perturbatively UV-finite: order by order, the extended nature of strings smooths out the UV divergences of point-particle QFT.

It predicts supersymmetry, extra dimensions, and a vast landscape of possible vacuum states ($\sim 10^{500}$ vacua).

It has not been experimentally confirmed.

Loop Quantum Gravity:

Quantizes spacetime geometry directly.

The fundamental excitations are not particles or strings but discrete loops of quantum geometry, spin networks and spin foams.

Area and volume become quantized:

\[A_{min} = 4\pi\gamma\sqrt{3}\,\ell_P^2\]

where $\gamma \approx 0.2375$ is the Barbero-Immirzi parameter.

Spacetime at the Planck scale is a discrete foam of quantum geometry, not a smooth manifold but a combinatorial structure.

LQG is background-independent: it does not assume a fixed spacetime background. It attempts to quantize spacetime itself.

It has not been experimentally confirmed.

Causal Dynamical Triangulations (CDT):

A non-perturbative approach to quantum gravity using a path integral over causal geometries, triangulated spacetime manifolds.

Numerical simulations suggest that the effective dimension of spacetime runs with scale: close to 4 at large distances, falling to roughly 2 near the Planck scale, a phenomenon called dimensional reduction.

Asymptotic Safety:

Proposes that gravity has a non-trivial UV fixed point, a Planck-scale fixed point of the renormalization group, at which it becomes non-perturbatively renormalizable.

If the gravitational coupling flows to a fixed point, quantum gravity is well-defined without new physics at the Planck scale.

None of these theories is confirmed. None makes predictions accessible to current experiment.

IX. The Generalized Uncertainty Principle

Most quantum gravity approaches predict a modification of the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, a Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP):

\[\Delta x \Delta p \geq rac{\hbar}{2}\left(1 + eta rac{\ell_P^2}{\hbar^2}(\Delta p)^2 ight)\]

where $ eta$ is a dimensionless parameter of order unity in most models.

This modification introduces a minimum length:

\[\Delta x_{min} = \ell_P\sqrt{ eta}\]

The GUP has consequences:

Modified dispersion relations:

\[E^2 = p^2c^2 + m^2c^4 + \alpha rac{E^3}{E_P} + ...\]

Modified thermodynamics: Black hole thermodynamics is modified near the Planck scale. The Hawking temperature receives corrections:

\[T_H = rac{\hbar c^3}{8\pi G M k_B}\left(1 - \alpha rac{m_P^2}{M^2} ight)\]

Minimum black hole mass: Black holes cannot evaporate completely: they leave a Planck-mass remnant. This has implications for the black hole information paradox.

Modified uncertainty in quantum mechanics: Standard quantum mechanics receives corrections at very high momenta. These corrections are unmeasurably small for current experiments, but in principle observable.

X. What We Don’t Know, Honestly

Let me be direct about the state of the field.

We have no confirmed theory of quantum gravity.

Not “we’re close but need more work.”

We have several candidate frameworks, none of which makes predictions that have been tested.

We have beautiful mathematics, in string theory, in LQG, in CDT, but mathematics is not physics until it makes contact with experiment.

The Planck scale is experimentally inaccessible by direct probing, and indirect constraints have not yet revealed any deviation from our current theories.

Lorentz invariance holds. CPT holds. Our theories keep working down to scales of $\sim 10^{-18}$ m, seventeen orders of magnitude above the Planck scale, but still.

The cosmological constant problem remains unsolved.

This is possibly the deepest problem in physics. It connects the Planck scale to cosmology in a way we do not understand.

We do not know if spacetime is continuous or discrete.

We do not know if Lorentz invariance holds exactly at the Planck scale or is merely an emergent low-energy approximation.

We do not know if the Planck length is truly the minimum length or merely the scale at which our current understanding fails.

These are no details. They are foundational.

XI. Why This Should Matter to You

The Planck scale is not relevant to daily life. It is not relevant to quantum computing. It is not relevant to condensed matter physics, to chemistry, to biology.

It is relevant to one thing:

The question of what reality is.

At the Planck scale, the question “what is spacetime made of?” becomes empirical rather than philosophical.

And we do not know the answer.

We live in a universe whose deepest structure is unknown to us.

Not unknown in the sense of not yet measured, unknown in the sense of our best theories breaking down before we get there.

The Planck scale is the place where the infinite regress of “what is X made of?” reaches the edge of the knowable.

Beyond it: not darkness, exactly. Not ignorance, exactly.

The known unknown.

The place where our map ends and the territory continues without us.

Coda

In 1899, Planck computed these units as a mathematical curiosity.

He noted that they were natural, free of human convention, and published them the following year in a paper on irreversible radiation processes.

He did not know he was identifying the edge of physics.

He did not know that a century later, the units he computed as an aside would define the boundary between what we know and what we cannot yet know.

The Planck length is $10^{-35}$ meters. The proton is $10^{-15}$ meters. The Planck length is twenty orders of magnitude smaller than the proton.

Twenty orders of magnitude of unknown.

We are very far from the edge.

We are also, in some sense, always at the edge, because the edge is where we are going, and the going is the physics.

Further reading:

Planck, “Über irreversible Strahlungsvorgänge” (1899/1900) Presented to the Prussian Academy in 1899, published in Annalen der Physik in 1900. The original paper containing Planck units.

Garay, “Quantum gravity and minimum length” (1995) Int. J. Mod. Phys. A 10, 145 The definitive review of minimum length.

Rovelli, Quantum Gravity (2004) Cambridge University Press The LQG textbook.

Polchinski, String Theory (1998) Cambridge University Press The string theory bible.

For the cosmological constant problem:

Weinberg, “The cosmological constant problem” (1989) Rev. Mod. Phys. 61, 1 Still the best review after 35 years.
entry.summary: At 10⁻³⁵ meters, our best theories break down simultaneously. This is the edge of what we can know, not a technical problem.

entry.title: The Fine-Tuned Universe: Why the Constants Are What They Are

link.title: The Fine-Tuned Universe: Why the Constants Are What They Are

entry.content:
There are numbers written into the fabric of the universe.

Not derived from any deeper principle. Not explained by any known theory. Simply measured!

The fine structure constant:

\[\alpha = rac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c} \approx 1/137.036\]

The ratio of proton to electron mass:

\[m_p/m_e \approx 1836.15\]

The cosmological constant:

\[\Lambda \approx 1.1 imes 10^{-52} ext{ m}^{-2}\]

The strength of gravity relative to electromagnetism:

\[\alpha_G/\alpha \approx 10^{-36}\]

These numbers have no explanation. They are what they are.

And if any of them were slightly different, not vastly different, slightly, the universe would contain no stars, no chemistry, no complexity, no life. (Yes!)

This is the fine-tuning problem.

It is either:

(a) the most profound clue about the nature of reality

(b) a selection effect masquerading as a deep truth

(c) evidence for a multiverse

(d) evidence for design

(e) a pseudo-problem that dissolves under scrutiny

Physicists disagree, fiercely, about which. :)

I will show you why all of these answers have something to recommend them and something deeply wrong with them.

I. The Constants of Nature

Including the neutrino sector, the Standard Model has 25 free parameters:

  • 6 quark masses: \(m_u, m_d, m_s, m_c, m_b, m_t\)
  • 3 charged lepton masses: \(m_e, m_\mu, m_ au\)
  • 3 neutrino masses: \(m_{ u_1}, m_{ u_2}, m_{ u_3}\)
  • 4 CKM mixing parameters (quark mixing)
  • 4 PMNS mixing parameters (neutrino mixing)
  • 3 gauge coupling constants: \(g_1, g_2, g_3\)
  • 1 Higgs quartic coupling: \(\lambda\)
  • 1 Higgs mass parameter: \(\mu^2\)

Plus gravity adds:

  • Newton’s constant: \(G\)
  • Cosmological constant: \(\Lambda\)

27 free parameters in total.

None of these is predicted by the theory. All must be measured.

The theory gives us the framework. The universe fills in the numbers.

Why these numbers? We don’t know.

II. The Evidence for Fine-Tuning

Let me be precise about what fine-tuning claims.

It does not claim: these values were chosen by a designer.

It does not claim: they could not have been different.

It claims: small changes to these values would produce a universe qualitatively different. Specifically, a universe without complex structures.

Let me give the most compelling examples.

1. The Strong Force: Carbon and Oxygen

Carbon is the basis of chemistry as we know it. It forms stable molecules. It enables the complexity of life.

Carbon is synthesized in stellar interiors via the triple-alpha process:

\(^4 ext{He} + ^4 ext{He} o ^8 ext{Be}\) \(^8 ext{Be} + ^4 ext{He} o ^{12} ext{C} + \gamma\)

The problem: \(^8\)Be is unstable. It decays in \(\sim 10^{-16}\) s.

The reaction proceeds only because carbon-12 has a resonance at exactly the right energy: the Hoyle state at 7.6549 MeV.

Fred Hoyle predicted this resonance in 1953 before it was measured, reasoning that carbon must exist (since we exist), therefore carbon-12 must have this resonance.

The resonance energy is extraordinarily sensitive to the nuclear force coupling.

Change the strong force by \(\sim 0.4\%\) stronger: \(^8\)Be becomes stable. All helium burns to carbon in the Big Bang. No hydrogen remains, no water, no biochemistry.

Change it by \(\sim 0.4\%\) weaker: the Hoyle state is off-resonance. Almost no carbon produced in stars. No carbon-based chemistry.

A window of \(\sim 0.8\%\) in the strong coupling permits carbon to exist.

This was the observation that most impressed Freeman Dyson and Fred Hoyle, both skeptical scientists, neither inclined toward teleology.

Hoyle wrote (1981):

“A commonsense interpretation of the facts suggests that a superintellect has monkeyed with physics, as well as with chemistry and biology, and that there are no blind forces worth speaking about in nature.”

He was not endorsing design. He was expressing how striking the coincidence seemed.

2. The Cosmological Constant: Structure Formation

We have discussed \(\Lambda\) extensively. Here its fine-tuning is most acute.

For structure to form in the universe: gravitational attraction must overcome the accelerating expansion driven by \(\Lambda\).

If \(\Lambda\) is too large: the universe expands too fast for density perturbations to grow into galaxies.

The condition for structure formation:

\[ ho_\Lambda \lesssim ho_m(z_{eq})\]

where \(z_{eq}\) is the redshift of matter-radiation equality.

This requires:

\[\Lambda \lesssim 10^{-120} m_P^4\]

The “natural” value: \(\sim m_P^4\).

Fine-tuning required: \(10^{120}\).

The most severe fine-tuning in all of physics.

3. The Higgs Mass and Electroweak Scale

The electroweak scale \(v \approx 246\) GeV sets the masses of:

  • The W and Z bosons: \(\sim 80 ext{-}90\) GeV
  • The electron mass: \(\sim 0.5\) MeV (via Yukawa)
  • The proton mass: indirectly, via QCD running

The electroweak scale must be:

  • Small enough for hydrogen to be stable (proton must not decay to positron + neutron)
  • Large enough for carbon chemistry
  • Consistent with a stable vacuum

If \(v \gg 246\) GeV: quarks are too heavy, protons unstable.

If \(v \ll 246\) GeV: electrons and protons nearly the same mass, hydrogen is unstable.

The window for stable atoms containing hydrogen:

\[v \in [100, 10^4] ext{ GeV}\]

roughly speaking.

The actual value sits within this window, but the naturalness problem asks: why isn’t \(v \sim m_P = 10^{19}\) GeV, as quantum corrections would naively suggest?

4. The Proton-Electron Mass Ratio

\[\mu = m_p/m_e \approx 1836\]

If \(\mu \ll 1836\): electrons are too heavy relative to protons. Molecular bonds weaken. Chemistry is less stable.

If \(\mu \gg 1836\): atomic nuclei are essentially fixed points. Molecular vibrations change character. Complex chemistry is disrupted.

The window for Earth-like chemistry: roughly \(\mu \in [10^2, 10^4]\).

The actual value: 1836.

5. The Electromagnetic Coupling

\[\alpha \approx 1/137\]

If \(\alpha\) is larger:

  • Atoms are smaller (Bohr radius \(\propto 1/\alpha\))
  • Stars burn faster (nuclear reaction rates \(\propto \alpha^2\))
  • Stellar lifetimes shorter

If \(\alpha\) is much smaller:

  • Chemistry weaker (molecular bonds weaker)
  • Complex molecules less stable

The window for long-lived stars and stable chemistry: roughly a factor of 10 either way.

6. The Dimensionality of Space

This is less often discussed but equally striking.

Why 3 spatial dimensions?

In \(d = 2\): gravity falls as \(1/r\), no stable planetary orbits (no closed orbits, only spiraling).

In \(d \geq 4\): gravity falls faster than \(1/r^2\), no stable planetary orbits (all orbits unstable).

The Ehrenfest argument (1917): only in \(d = 3\) do stable closed orbits exist under an inverse-square force.

Similarly:

  • Wave equations have sharp signals only in odd dimensions
  • The Laplace equation has physical properties specific to \(d = 3\)

Whether this is fine-tuning or a theorem about which dimensions permit observers is debated.

III. Quantifying Fine-Tuning

How do we measure fine-tuning?

Sensitivity measure:

\[\Delta_i = \left\lvert rac{\partial \ln O}{\partial \ln c_i} ight vert\]

where \(O\) is some observable (e.g., existence of carbon) and \(c_i\) is the constant being varied.

Large \(\Delta_i\): \(O\) is sensitive to \(c_i\), fine-tuned. Small \(\Delta_i\): \(O\) is insensitive, robust.

Probabilistic measure:

If the constants are drawn from some distribution, what is the probability of a life-permitting universe?

This requires:

  1. A prior distribution over constant values
  2. A definition of “life-permitting”
  3. A measure on the space of universes

None of these is well-defined. The probabilistic argument is only as good as the assumptions about the distribution.

This is the measure problem. And it is severe.

IV. The Anthropic Principle

The Weak Anthropic Principle (WAP):

“The observed values of all physical and cosmological quantities are not equally probable, but they take on values restricted by the requirement that there exist sites where carbon-based life can evolve and by the requirement that the universe be old enough for it to have already done so.”

Barrow & Tipler (1986)

The WAP is trivially true and philosophically important.

Trivially true: we can only observe a universe where we exist to observe it.

Philosophically important: it changes the question.

Instead of asking: “Why does our universe have these constants?”

We ask: “Given that we exist, what is the expected distribution of constants we should observe?”

This reframes fine-tuning as a selection effect.

The Strong Anthropic Principle (SAP):

“The universe must have those properties which allow life to develop within it at some stage in its history.”

This is much more controversial. It implies the constants are necessarily what they are, which requires either:

  • A teleological principle (purpose in nature)
  • A multiverse with observer selection
  • A deeper theory that fixes the constants

The SAP in its strongest form is not scientific. It is not falsifiable.

V. The Multiverse: The Physicist’s Answer

If there exists a vast ensemble of universes, each with different values of the fundamental constants, then the fine-tuning is explained by selection:

We live in a universe with life-permitting constants because we could not live in one without them.

String theory landscape:

String theory predicts \(\sim 10^{500}\) metastable vacua, different compactifications of the extra dimensions, each giving different effective physics.

Different vacua have different:

  • Values of \(\Lambda\)
  • Gauge groups and matter content
  • Coupling constants

If all vacua are realized, if the landscape is populated by eternal inflation, bubble nucleation, then the anthropic selection explains why we observe a small \(\Lambda\).

Weinberg’s 1987 prediction of the cosmological constant (using anthropic reasoning before its discovery) is the strongest argument for this approach.

Problems with the multiverse:

Untestability:

Other universes are, by definition, causally disconnected from ours. No observation can confirm or deny their existence.

The multiverse is not a scientific hypothesis in the Popperian sense. It cannot be falsified.

The measure problem:

Even granting the multiverse, how do we calculate probabilities? What is the probability distribution over vacua?

There are infinitely many universes with each value of each constant. Comparing infinities requires a measure, and there is no agreed measure on the landscape.

Typicality:

Why should we be “typical” observers in the multiverse?

The Boltzmann brain problem: in an infinite universe, fluctuations will spontaneously create observers (Boltzmann brains) who falsely believe they exist in a structured universe.

If Boltzmann brains are more numerous than ordinary observers, and in an infinite universe they may be, then the typical observer is a Boltzmann brain, not us.

This is absurd. But not obviously wrong.

The string landscape is not a unique prediction:

Any theory that predicts a vast number of vacua can be used to “explain” any observed constants anthropically.

This is too easy. A theory that can explain anything predicts nothing.

VI. The Designer Hypothesis

Fine-tuning is often cited as evidence for design, for a universe created by an intelligent agent who set the constants to permit life.

This is the argument from fine-tuning in contemporary natural theology.

As a physicist, I want to assess this argument on its merits, not dismiss it.

The argument:

  1. The constants are fine-tuned for life.
  2. Fine-tuning is more probable given design than given chance.
  3. Therefore, design is more probable than chance.

This is a Bayesian argument. It has the form of a valid inference.

The problems:

What is the prior?

To say fine-tuning is more probable given design, we need a prior over possible designers and their intentions.

Why would a designer create a universe with exactly one life-permitting pocket in \(10^{500}\) possible vacua? Why not set the constants so all possible values permit life?

A designer who created only one life-permitting universe in a vast space of sterile universes is not obviously more plausible than no designer.

The explanation bottoms out:

If fine-tuned constants require an explanation, a designer, then the designer requires an explanation.

What designed the designer?

Either we accept an unexplained explainer (which could equally be the universe itself) or we face an infinite regress.

Selection bias:

The designer hypothesis does not explain why we observe this universe rather than any other life-permitting universe a designer might create.

It predicts a life-permitting universe. So does the multiverse + anthropic selection. The observations do not distinguish them.

I am not asserting the designer hypothesis is wrong. I am asserting it does not resolve the explanatory problem. It relocates it.

VII. The Alternative: A Deeper Theory

The most scientifically satisfying resolution:

The constants are not free parameters.

A more fundamental theory, unknown to us, derives the constants from deeper principles.

They appear fine-tuned because we don’t yet understand why they have the values they do.

Once we find the deeper theory, the constants will be seen to be necessary, or at least strongly constrained.

Historical precedent:

Before quantum mechanics, the Bohr model of hydrogen had a quantization condition:

\[L = n\hbar\]

This seemed arbitrary.

Quantum mechanics derived it from the wave nature of the electron. What seemed like fine-tuning became a theorem.

Before QCD, the charge quantization \(e\) seemed arbitrary.

In unified theories (GUTs), charge quantization follows from the group structure of the unified gauge group.

Perhaps the 27 free parameters are analogously fixed by a deeper theory.

String theory’s promise and failure:

String theory was supposed to fix all constants.

In the 1980s, string theorists hoped the theory would predict a unique vacuum with the SM constants determined by the math.

Instead: the landscape of \(10^{500}\) vacua.

The dream of a unique prediction gave way to the multiverse.

This is either:

physics discovering that the landscape is real, or physics failing to find the unique vacuum, or both simultaneously.

VIII. The Dirac Large Number Hypothesis

Paul Dirac noticed (1937):

The ratio of the electromagnetic force to gravity:

\[ rac{e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0}{Gm_e m_p} \approx 10^{39}\]

The age of the universe in atomic units:

\[ rac{t_{universe}}{e^2/m_e c^3} \approx 10^{39}\]

The ratio of the observable universe to the classical electron radius:

\[ rac{R_{universe}}{r_e} \approx 10^{39}\]

Three completely different ratios, all approximately \(10^{39}\).

Is this coincidence?

Dirac thought not. He proposed that these large numbers are related by a deeper principle, and that some “constants” must vary with time to maintain the coincidence as the universe ages.

If \(G \propto 1/t\): the gravitational constant decreases with time.

This prediction has been tested. No variation of \(G\) is observed at the level of \(\dot{G}/G \lesssim 10^{-13}\) yr\(^{-1}\).

Dirac’s hypothesis is ruled out in its original form.

But the large number coincidences remain unexplained.

Carter’s anthropic response:

Brandon Carter (1974) argued: the coincidence \(N_1 \sim N_2 \sim N_3 \sim 10^{39}\) is not a deep law but an anthropic selection effect.

Observers can only exist at cosmic times when the conditions for biology are met. These conditions require:

  • Stars exist (not yet formed, or already dead)
  • The universe is not yet dominated by \(\Lambda\)

This selects \(t \sim t_{stellar} \sim \sqrt{\alpha^5/\alpha_G} \cdot t_P \sim 10^{10}\) yr.

At this time, the coincidence holds.

The coincidence tells us when observers exist, not what the fundamental laws are.

IX. The Landscape of Possible Physics

Let me take a step back and ask a different question:

How large is the space of possible universes?

We can parametrize:

  • The gauge group (infinitely many possibilities)
  • The matter content (infinitely many)
  • The number of spacetime dimensions (any integer)
  • The values of all coupling constants (continuous)
  • The topology of spacetime (infinitely many)

The space of possible physics is enormous, perhaps infinite.

In this vast space, what fraction of universes permits complexity?

Tegmark’s analysis:

Max Tegmark systematically analyzed the allowed region of parameter space (varying \(\alpha\), \(\alpha_G\), \(m_e/m_p\), \(m_n - m_p\)).

The life-permitting region: a small fraction of the total parameter space, but not vanishingly small.

The region where:

  • Atoms are stable
  • Stars have long enough lifetimes
  • Chemistry is rich enough for life

is approximately:

\(\Omega_{life} \sim 10^{-3}\) to \(10^{-10}\)

of the natural parameter space.

Whether \(10^{-10}\) constitutes “fine-tuning” requiring explanation, or is simply a small but not extraordinary number, is partly a matter of definition.

X. What We Actually Know

Let me distinguish:

Established:

  1. The constants have specific measured values.

  2. Small changes to some constants produce qualitatively different universes, universes without atoms, without stars, without complex chemistry.

  3. We have no theory that derives the constants from first principles.

  4. The cosmological constant is \(10^{120}\) times smaller than the natural QFT estimate.

Contested:

  1. Whether the sensitivity of life to constants constitutes “fine-tuning” requiring explanation depends on the measure you use.

  2. Whether a multiverse exists and whether it resolves the fine-tuning is not established.

  3. Whether a unique theory will derive the constants is unknown.

Unknown:

  1. Why these values and not others.

  2. Whether the constants could have been different.

  3. What “could have been different” means in the absence of a theory of initial conditions.

XI. The Deepest Question

Fine-tuning points to a question that physics cannot currently answer, and may never answer:

Why is there something rather than nothing? And why is the something the way it is?

Leibniz asked this in 1714. We have not answered it.

The fine-tuning observations show: the something is not arbitrary. It has specific, calibrated structure that permits complexity.

Whether this requires an explanation, or whether it is the kind of brute fact that terminates explanation, is not a scientific question.

It is a philosophical one.

And the physicists who insist that “the multiverse explains it” or that “a deeper theory will derive it” or that “it’s just anthropic selection” are making philosophical commitments. Not scientific ones.

All of them might be right. None of them can currently be tested.

The fine-tuning of the universe is the place where physics runs out of physics, and becomes something else.

Philosophy. Cosmology. Metaphysics. Perhaps theology.

( My dear reader please, do not get mad at me. It’s all because I read too much Popper! Ahahaha, fan girl Filizco!) :)

The honest scientist acknowledges this edge.

Does not pretend it is not there. Does not jump over it with speculative physics.

Stands at the edge and says:

Here is what we know. Here is where knowledge ends. The question remains open. We are working on it.

That is the scientific posture. It is also the only honest one.

Coda

The universe did not have to be this way.

Or maybe it did.

We do not know which.

What we know is this:

The universe we inhabit is one in which stars burn for billions of years, carbon forms in stellar cores, planets orbit at stable distances, water is liquid at the right temperatures, electrons and protons form stable atoms, atoms form molecules of arbitrary complexity, and somewhere on a small planet around an unremarkable star, the molecules organized themselves into something that could look up and ask why.

Whether that last step was inevitable, whether the constants were set precisely so that asking would eventually be possible,

is the question.

We do not know the answer.

But the asking itself, the fact that the universe produced something capable of wondering about its own structure,

is the most remarkable consequence of whatever the answer turns out to be.

Essential reading:

Barrow & Tipler. The Anthropic Cosmological Principle (1986). Comprehensive; the standard reference.

Rees. Just Six Numbers (1999). Accessible; the best popular account.

Weinberg. “Anthropic Bound on the Cosmological Constant” (1987). Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 2607. The prediction.

Susskind. The Cosmic Landscape (2005). The string landscape argument; readable.

Smolin. The Life of the Cosmos (1997). Cosmological natural selection; alternative to anthropics.

Tegmark. “On the dimensionality of spacetime” (1997). Class. Quant. Grav. 14, L69. Quantitative fine-tuning analysis.

For the philosophical dimension:

Leslie. Universes (1989). The philosophical analysis.

Sober. “The Design Argument” in Blackwell Guide to the Philosophy of Religion (2003). The best critical analysis of design arguments.

Carter. “Large Number Coincidences and the* Anthropic Principle in Cosmology” *(1974). IAU Symposium 63, 291. Where the anthropic principle was formalized.
entry.summary: The fundamental constants of nature appear to be precisely calibrated for the existence of complexity. Change any of them slightly, and the universe becomes sterile. This is either the deepest fact about reality, or the most dangerous idea in physics.

entry.title: The Problem of the Self: Does “You” Exist?

link.title: The Problem of the Self: Does “You” Exist?

entry.content:
You are reading this sentence.

Behind your eyes, something is happening, a process, an experience, a witnessing. There is, it seems, a you doing the reading.

This seems like the most obvious fact in the world. Descartes built his entire philosophy on it: cogito ergo sum, I think, therefore I am.

The I is the one thing we cannot doubt.

I want to suggest that Descartes was wrong. Not about the thinking, about the I.

Hume’s Bundle Theory

In 1739, David Hume sat down and tried to introspect on his own self.

He expected to find, as most people assume, some stable, continuous entity. The “I” that persists through time. The subject of all experience.

What he found instead:

“When I enter most intimately into what I call myself, I always stumble on some particular perception or other, of heat or cold, light or shade, love or hatred, pain or pleasure. I never catch myself at any time without a perception, and can never observe anything but the perception.”

There is no self behind the perceptions. Only the perceptions themselves, a constant stream of sensations, thoughts, emotions, memories.

Hume called this the bundle theory of the self: the self is not a thing, it is a bundle of perceptions, held together by nothing more than memory and habit.

The “I” is a grammatical convenience, not a metaphysical entity.

The Ship of Theseus, Turned Inward

The ancient paradox: if you replace every plank of a ship, is it still the same ship?

Now turn this inward.

The atoms in your body replace themselves continuously. Every seven to ten years, most of your cells are new. The neurons in your brain rewire constantly, new synaptic connections formed, old ones pruned. Your beliefs, memories, values, personality, all of these have changed since childhood.

What exactly is the thing that persists?

You might say: memory. The continuous narrative thread.

But memories are reconstructive, not reproductive. Every time you remember something, you are not retrieving a stored file, you are rebuilding it from fragments, influenced by everything that has happened since.

Your memory of your childhood is not your childhood. It is a present-day reconstruction, wearing the costume of the past.

Parfit and What Matters in Survival

Derek Parfit’s Reasons and Persons (1984) is one of the most important philosophy books of the twentieth century, and one of the least read outside academic philosophy.

Parfit’s central question: what matters in survival?

He approached it through thought experiments.

Teletransportation: Suppose a machine scans every atom of your body, destroys the original, and recreates a perfect copy on Mars, same memories, same personality, same beliefs.

Is the person on Mars you?

Most people’s intuition: no. The original was destroyed. The Martian is a copy.

But Parfit asks: what if the machine malfunctions slightly, and doesn’t destroy the original? Now there are two of you, one on Earth, one on Mars. They are equally connected to your past self. Which one is you?

Neither can be, there can’t be two of you. But both have equal claim.

Parfit’s conclusion: personal identity is not what matters.

What matters is psychological continuity, the overlapping chains of memory, intention, belief, and character that connect your past self to your future self.

But these connections come in degrees. They can branch. They can fade. There is no sharp line where you begin and end.

The self is not a thing. It is a degree of connectedness.

And once you see this clearly, Parfit argued, it is deeply liberating.

The fear of death, properly understood, is the fear of the self’s dissolution. But if the self was never a unified, persistent thing to begin with, if it was always a process, always a matter of degree, then what exactly are you afraid of losing?

The Buddhist Diagnosis

Twenty-five centuries before Parfit, the Buddha arrived at the same conclusion.

The doctrine of anātman (Sanskrit) or anattā (Pāli): there is no permanent, unchanging self.

What we call the self is a collection of five aggregates (skandhas):

  1. Rūpa: form, the physical body
  2. Vedanā: sensation, feeling tone (pleasant/unpleasant/neutral)
  3. Saññā: perception, recognition
  4. Saṅkhāra: mental formations, volitions, habits
  5. Viññāṇa: consciousness, awareness

None of these is the self. The self is what arises when they interact, a process, not a substance.

The Buddha’s diagnosis: dukkha, suffering, dissatisfaction, arises from clinging to a self that was never there. We grasp at a fixed identity, resist change, build elaborate structures to protect an “I” that is more verb than noun.

The Buddhist path is not the annihilation of the self. It is the seeing through of the illusion, and the freedom that follows.

What is remarkable is that this is not mysticism. It is careful phenomenological analysis, arrived at through sustained introspective practice.

Hume would have recognized it immediately.

What Neuroscience Says

The neuroscientific picture is, if anything, more vertiginous.

The brain does not have a central processing unit, a “seat of the self” where everything comes together. Consciousness is not located anywhere in particular.

The default mode network (DMN), a set of brain regions active during self-referential thought, mind-wandering, and narrative construction, is sometimes called the “self network.” But it is a network, not a center. It is distributed, dynamic, constantly changing.

Benjamin Libet’s experiments (1983): subjects were asked to flex their wrist whenever they chose, and report the moment of conscious decision. The brain’s readiness potential, a measurable buildup of neural activity, preceded the reported moment of conscious decision by approximately 350 milliseconds.

The brain had already begun the movement before the subject decided to move.

If the conscious “I” did not initiate the action, if the decision was already underway before awareness of it, what role is the self playing?

Perhaps: narrator, not agent. The self may be a story the brain tells about itself, after the fact, to create the illusion of unified authorship.

You are not the driver. You are the passenger writing a real-time account of a journey that began before you picked up the pen.

The Paradox of the Introspecting Subject

Here is the deepest difficulty.

To investigate the self, you use the self. To question the “I,” an “I” does the questioning.

This is not merely circular, it is constitutively so. There is no view from nowhere. Every act of introspection is performed by the very thing under investigation.

Kant saw this and concluded the self, the transcendental unity of apperception, must be presupposed as the condition of all experience. You cannot step outside it. It is the frame, not the picture.

But the frame shapes what you see.

Living Without a Self

What are the practical consequences of taking this seriously?

Parfit wrote that when he fully absorbed the implications of his own view, his life changed:

“When I believed that my existence was such a further fact, I seemed imprisoned in myself. My life seemed like a glass tunnel, through which I was moving faster every year, and at the end of which there was darkness. When I changed my view, the walls of my glass tunnel disappeared. I now live in the open air.”

The dissolution of the self, not as a metaphysical claim but as a lived reality, is the goal of contemplative traditions from Buddhism to Stoicism to certain strands of Christian mysticism.

Marcus Aurelius:

“Things themselves touch not the soul, not in the least degree, nor have they admission to the soul, nor can they turn or move the soul; but the soul turns and moves itself alone.”

Epictetus:

“Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.”

These are not mere platitudes. They are practical consequences of a metaphysics, the Stoic view that the self is not identical to the body, the reputation, the career, the opinions of others. The self, properly understood, is rational agency. And rational agency cannot be taken from you.

Where This Leaves Us

Does the self exist?

The honest answer: not in the way you think it does.

There is experience. There is continuity of a kind. There is a perspective, a point of view.

But the unified, persistent, indivisible “I”, the Cartesian subject, the soul, the ghost in the machine, this does not survive scrutiny.

Hume didn’t find it. Parfit dissolved it. The Buddha saw through it. Neuroscience cannot locate it.

And yet, here you are, reading this, with the overwhelming sense that someone is reading.

Perhaps that sense is itself the answer. Not the self as substance, but the self as process. Not a noun, but a verb.

Not I am, but there is experiencing.

And maybe, just maybe, that is enough to go on with.

Further reading:

Derek Parfit. Reasons and Persons (1984).

David Hume. A Treatise of Human Nature (1739).

Thomas Metzinger. Being No One (2003).

Antonio Damasio. The Feeling of What Happens (1999).

Bhikkhu Bodhi. In the Buddha’s Words (2005).
entry.summary: Hume, Parfit, Buddhism, and the unsettling possibility that nobody is home.

entry.title: On an MRI Machine, a Forgotten Memory, and the Most Important Thing I Have Learned About Myself

link.title: On an MRI Machine, a Forgotten Memory, and the Most Important Thing I Have Learned About Myself

entry.content:
Three years ago I went to a routine eye appointment.

I wear glasses. Every six months, a check-up. Nothing special.

The doctor was looking at medical images of my retina when she paused.

She asked if I got headaches.

I said yes, always! I drink a lot of caffeine, I don’t drink enough water, I have sleep problems.

I had normalized the headaches a long time ago…

Then a second doctor came into the room. Then a third.

Each one looked at the screen, said hello to me, and turned back to the images.

I watched all of this and told myself:

eyyy, filizco, it’s nothing, do not worry about it!

tabii ki böyle demedim, konuşsanıza amk diye saydırdım içimden.

One of them asked if I had numbness in my arms or hands.

I said yes, actually. I did.

They spoke quietly among themselves. Then they told me: my prescription had changed significantly, and there was inflammation of the optic nerve. An MRI would be a good idea.

I tried to get more information. They said there could be many causes. The MRI would tell us more.

I walked out of the office and went directly to a café.

This is something I inherited from my grandmother. I never go straight home after difficult news.

When I was a child, after every doctor’s appointment she would take me to my favorite restaurant.

When I grew up and she was no longer with me, I kept the habit.

Find a crowded place first. Let your mind settle. Then go home.

I sat in the café and looked up what optic nerve inflammation could mean.

The first result: MS. Multiple sclerosis.

I sat with that for a while.

Then I called my closest friends.

My friend N started crying almost immediately. It’s her thing, and it is the exact reason why I love her.

Life is so unfair, Filiz. This is so unfair.

F said, “No, I don’t think it’s anything. I really don’t.”

But his voice, his whole energy on the phone, changed completely.

I knew him well enough to know he looked it up the moment we hung up.

M was at work that day. I texted him the news.

M called me a little later, after he had done his own research.

He is deeply religious. Faith is the center of his life.

But that day he was angry (very unusual of him).

I’m angry at God, Filiz. He hasn’t given you things other people take for granted, and now this on top of everything? He shouldn’t do this!

His voice broke a little.

I have had a great life. Hard one, yes, but genuinely, fully great.

I traveled the most beautiful places on earth, tasted the foods I wanted to try, always blessed with the best people. Ben dünyada olduğum için her zaman çok mutluydum!

If today were my last day, I would have no remorse about myself!

My closest friends know this about me!

I understood why they were reacting this way. They know my life.

They know that I have navigated most of it without the safety net that most people don’t even notice they have, the people who are simply there, who you don’t have to explain anything to, who would show up.

My friends are that for me now.

But they also know what it cost to get here. And they were frightened for someone who has already carried more than her share.

I listened to all of them. I told them it would be okay. I didn’t know yet if that was true, but it felt like the right thing to say.

Only later did I notice that I had spent those conversations on the other side of the equation.

The one doing the reassuring, not the one being reassured.

I didn’t mind. That is just how I am built.

But I also knew, somewhere, that I needed to be as careful with myself as my friends were being with me.

I may never fully come to terms with how unfair life is, but I accepted that truth a long time ago.

I have always tried to live fully in whatever moment I am in.

That is how my grandmother raised me!

For the MRI, they gave me an appointment for two weeks later.

I cannot explain how vulnerable you feel being far away from home when you are having such health problems.

I was not going to sit at home for two weeks feeling sorry for myself! Not for Filizko! :)

The week after the eye appointment, we bought tickets to New York. We flew there.

We strolled the city, ate incredible East Coast cuisine, visited every bookstore I loved, spent hours in museums in front of paintings I love.

We stayed in Hoboken and every morning I woke up to the Manhattan skyline.

Most of the time, I was having fun. NYC is the kind of city that pulls you in, that makes you forget.

The MS thought came back occasionally.

If you have MS, you can collapse suddenly. That was frightening. But if I had MS, there was nothing I could do about it. I would only know when I knew.

What unsettled me more was the fear that came into M’s eyes, every now and then, when he thought I wasn’t looking.

It was chilling.

I was okay with waiting. He was not!

He was ready to do anything, to learn the truth immediately…

He was in NYC with me, but his brain had no break until exam day!

Then came the MRI day!

There was a problem.

The machine was not the kind where only your head goes in. My whole body had to be inside.

I have claustrophobia.
