I undressed completely. They gave me a white garment: ugly, unironed, freshly washed.

I lay down on the table. The machine began to move slowly, pulling me inside.

A few minutes in, I said I needed to get out. I was breathing too fast.

The technician said: I don’t think we can do this, you’re not looking well.

I really couldn’t. My heart was trying to leave my chest.

It’s a terrible machine, it makes terrible sounds and you cannot move at all.

But I genuinely needed to know. Whether I had MS or not.

The uncertainty was one thing. I can tolerate uncertainty. But this uncertainty was different.

I said: I’ll do it.

I lay back down. The technician said: I don’t think this is going to work, but okay, let’s try one more time.

I closed my eyes. I did not open them for one hour.

I could feel tears wanting to come but I held them.

I was going to learn the truth, whatever it was.

My heart was beating loud enough to feel in my chest for the first four or five minutes.

And then, from somewhere, a memory came.

Something I hadn’t thought about in twenty-four years.

My grandmother had surgery once, when I was a child. I stayed with my aunt during that time.

When we went to visit her afterward, I asked: Grandma, what did they do to you?

She told me they put her in a closed machine for a long time, then operated, removed the bad things.

She had serious heart problems and had gone through open-heart surgery.

I asked: Weren’t you scared? In the closed machine?

She said: I was scared. But then I thought of you, and it passed.

That memory came to me in the machine.

I thought: She was scared too. She thought of me and it passed. I’m scared. I’ll think of her.

It will pass. A few more minutes. You’re almost there, Filiz.

When the sixty minutes ended, the white garment was soaked through.

The technician said: I thought you couldn’t do it. You’re a pretty tough lady.

A few weeks passed.

I did not pray to God. I do not know, I just could not…

Then the results came in.

It was not MS!!! (Yesss beeeh!!!)

It was something called pseudotumor cerebri.

Hypothyroidism and extra weight were putting pressure on my spine.

Not even a real tumor. There was treatment. There was a solution.

Everyone was very happy. I was happy too.

But I had learned something.

I needed to take better care of myself.

Everything outside of me, every obligation, every responsibility, every job, every person, was a fraction of my life.

The main thing was me!

Me » everything else.

I had always been sensitive to other people, always tried to help, always taken on more than I should.

But this moment was clear: I needed to take care of myself.

Physically. Psychologically. Emotionally.

I kept that promise to myself for a long time.

Then, being in a foreign country, the workload, the school, the pressure, somewhere the thread broke again.

Not as badly as before, but I still wasn’t meeting all my own needs.

A few weeks ago, my body reminded me again:

iron deficiency, heavy periods, heart palpitations, shortness of breath.

I remembered the girl in the MRI machine who held herself together for sixty minutes so she could learn the truth.

Don’t forget her, I told myself.

Your degree, your work, other people, all of it is a fraction of your life.

You come first, Filiz.

I don’t want my body to have to remind me again. And honestly, I do not know whether I am lucky enough to be reminded again. Not everyone has that chance, right?

I am grateful to God for those reminders.

So..

Everything else can wait. Everyone else can wait.

I am only going to spend my energy on things that make me happy, on things that move me toward a better version of myself.

I already don’t keep people around me who exhaust me.

But the ones I’ve felt obligated to, the ones who drain me for no real reason, I’m going to give them only what’s necessary.

Nothing more.

I love myself. I will love myself more!

I want to spend my life with the people and things that make me feel that.

No more chasing. No more fixing. No more running after things that aren’t already moving toward me.

My happiness is the most important debt I owe.

And I intend to pay it.
entry.summary: I owe myself happiness. This is how I learned that.

entry.title: What Is Time? Augustine, Heidegger, and the Physics of the Passing Moment

link.title: What Is Time? Augustine, Heidegger, and the Physics of the Passing Moment

entry.content:
Augustine of Hippo, in the year 397, wrote one of the most honest sentences in the history of philosophy:

“Quid est ergo tempus? Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio; si quaerenti explicare velim, nescio.”

“What then is time? If no one asks me, I know. If I want to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.”

He wrote this in the Confessions, a book that is itself a meditation on time, on memory, on the self that persists through the passing of moments.

He is right.

You know what time is in the way you know how to breathe. Without thinking about it, without being able to explain it.

The moment you try to explain it, the thing dissolves.

The present: where is it? By the time you name it, it is gone.

The past: it no longer exists. The future: it does not yet exist.

And yet time is the most real thing there is.

More real than space. More intimate than thought.

You are inside it right now. You cannot get out. You cannot examine it from outside.

This is the problem of time.

I. Augustine. Time as the Soul’s Extension

Augustine’s analysis of time in Book XI of the Confessions is the first great philosophical account of temporal experience.

His starting point: the cosmological question.

“What was God doing before the Creation?”

The naive answer: preparing hell for those who ask such questions. :) (Ahahhahahha!)

Augustine quotes this with gentle irony.

His real answer: the question is malformed.

Before the Creation, there was no time. Time was created with the world. “Before” requires time. There is no before.

“Et nullum tempus, antequam faceres aliquid, fuit, quoniam et ipsum tempus tu fecisti.”

“And no time was, before you made anything, since you yourself made time.”

This is a profound move: time is not the container in which events occur. Time is itself created. It is part of the universe, not the stage on which the universe performs.

Both Augustine and Einstein refuse to treat time as a fixed container that exists independently of everything else. Augustine gets there through theology, Einstein through mathematics. The reasoning is completely different. But the destination has an odd resemblance.

(Whether this counts as anticipation or coincidence is a fair question. I lean toward interesting coincidence.)

The three presents:

Augustine’s most famous contribution to the philosophy of time:

The past does not exist. It is gone. The future does not exist. It has not yet come. The present is a knife-edge. It passes before you can name it.

And yet: we experience all three.

How?

Through the soul.

“Praesens de praeteritis memoria, praesens de praesentibus contuitus, praesens de futuris expectatio.”

“The present of past things is memory, the present of present things is sight, the present of future things is expectation.”

The three modes of time are three modes of the soul’s attention:

Memory: the past held in the present.

Attention: the present grasped in the present.

Expectation: the future anticipated in the present.

All three are present. All three are in the soul.

Time is not out there in the world. It is in here, in the mind that holds past and future in its present attention.

“In te, anime meus, tempora metior.”

“In you, my soul, I measure time.”

This is Augustine’s radical claim: time is psychological.

Not in the sense that it is unreal, but in the sense that temporal experience is constituted by the mind’s activity of holding past, present, and future together.

The distension of the soul:

Augustine uses the word distentio, distension, stretching, to describe the soul’s temporal structure.

The soul is stretched across time. Pulled toward the past by memory, pulled toward the future by expectation, held at the present by attention.

(I have felt this. The soul stretched between what was and what might be, unable to rest in what is. Augustine named it correctly.)

This stretching is not comfortable. It is the source of anxiety, of the restlessness that Augustine describes in the Confessions’ most famous line:

“Inquietum est cor nostrum, donec requiescat in te.”

“Our heart is restless, until it rests in you.”

The restlessness is temporal. The soul stretched across past and future, unable to rest in the present, is the condition of temporal existence.

Rest, the Sabbath, eternity, is the release from distension.

II. Heidegger. Being-Toward-Death

Martin Heidegger’s Being and Time (1927) is the most ambitious philosophical work of the twentieth century.

It’s an attempt to ask, for the first time since the Greeks, the fundamental question:

What does it mean to be?

And his answer: to understand being, you must understand time.

Because being is temporal. Everything that is, is in time.

Heidegger’s fundamental concept: Dasein, being-there, the kind of being that we are.

Dasein is not a subject contemplating an object. It is not a mind inside a body. It is being-in-the-world, already thrown into a situation, already caring about things, already engaged before reflection begins.

Thrownness:

We did not choose to exist. We did not choose our time, our place, our language, our body.

We found ourselves thrown into a situation not of our choosing.

This is Geworfenheit, thrownness.

The facticity of existence: that I am here, now, this, without having chosen any of it.

The temporality of Dasein:

Dasein is always:

Coming from a past it did not choose (thrownness), moving toward a future it cannot avoid (projection), existing in a present shaped by both.

This is the temporal structure of human existence: ecstatic temporality, the “ek-stasis” (standing-outside) of existing always beyond the present moment, always relating to what was and what will be.

Being-toward-death:

Heidegger’s most radical claim:

Death is not an event that happens at the end. Death is a structure of existence. Now.

I am always being-toward-death, always living in the light of my finitude, always existing as the being for whom my existence is an issue.

This is what distinguishes Dasein from a stone or a tree: not consciousness, exactly, but the fact that my being matters to me, that I must take a stand on it, that I cannot be indifferent to whether I exist.

Authentic and inauthentic existence:

Most of the time, we flee from the awareness of finitude.

We lose ourselves in the das Man, the “they,” the anonymous public, doing what one does, thinking what one thinks, living as one lives.

This is inauthenticity, not moral failure, but the everyday flight from the anxiety of genuine selfhood.

(This is the most uncomfortable part of Heidegger for me. Because he is right. Most of what I do on any given day is what “one does.” The genuine choices are rarer than I like to think.)

Authentic existence: confronting death, owning your thrownness, choosing from the possibilities that are genuinely yours, not because they are chosen for you by the anonymous they.

Anxiety:

For Heidegger, the mood that reveals the true structure of existence is Angst, anxiety.

Not fear of a specific thing. Anxiety is anxiety about nothing. About existence itself. About the groundlessness of being. About the fact that I am here without justification or guarantee.

Anxiety strips away the comfortable securities of everyday life and reveals what is always already there: the finite, temporal, groundless structure of human existence.

This is not pathology. It is clarity.

“Der Tod ist die eigenste Möglichkeit des Daseins.”

“Death is the ownmost possibility of Dasein.”

III. The Physics of Time. What Science Says

Philosophy asks: what is time?

Physics answers, partially, strangely, in ways that deepen the mystery rather than resolve it.

Newton’s absolute time:

For Newton, time is absolute, true, and mathematical, flowing equably, without relation to anything external.

It is the background, the container, in which events occur.

The same time passes for everyone, everywhere. There is a universal now.

This is what common sense tells us.

It is wrong.

Special relativity. The relativity of simultaneity:

Einstein showed (1905): simultaneity is relative.

Two events simultaneous in one reference frame are not simultaneous in another.

There is no universal now. The “same moment” means nothing without specifying a reference frame.

Time dilation: moving clocks run slow.

A clock on a fast-moving spaceship ticks more slowly than a clock at rest.

Not as an illusion. Really!

The astronaut who travels at near-light-speed ages more slowly than the person who stays.

Time is not absolute. It is woven into spacetime, a four-dimensional manifold in which time and space are related by the Lorentz transformation.

General relativity. Time curves:

In the presence of mass and energy, spacetime curves. Time itself curves.

Gravitational time dilation: clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields.

A clock at sea level ticks more slowly than a clock on a mountain. Not by much. But measurably.

GPS satellites must account for this.

Near a black hole: time slows toward the event horizon. At the horizon: time stops, from the perspective of a distant observer.

The block universe:

The most radical implication of relativity:

The block universe, or eternalism, holds that past, present, and future all equally exist.

In special relativity, different observers disagree about which events are simultaneous. There is no preferred “now” that carves the four-dimensional spacetime into past and future.

If there is no preferred now, if “now” is relative to the observer, then the distinction between “things that exist (present)” and “things that no longer exist (past)” is also observer-dependent.

This is not the only interpretation. Presentism holds that only the present is real. The growing block theory holds that the past and present exist but the future does not.

These are live debates in the philosophy of physics.

(I find the block universe unsettling but genuinely hard to argue against. Which is probably how it should feel.)

The arrow of time:

If the laws of physics are time-symmetric, if the equations of QM and GR look the same run forwards and backwards, why does time have a direction?

Why do we remember the past but not the future? Why do broken eggs not reassemble? Why does entropy increase?

The arrow of time is associated with entropy increase. But why entropy was low at the Big Bang, and why this produces our experience of time’s direction, remains genuinely open.

The universe began in an improbable, low-entropy configuration. Everything since has been moving toward greater disorder.

This is the direction we call “future.”

But the deeper question, why that initial condition, cannot be answered from within the physics.

The Planck time:

At \(t_P \approx 5.39 \times 10^{-44}\) seconds, the Planck time, our physics breaks down.

Before the Planck time after the Big Bang: the concept of time may not apply.

Quantum gravity, which we do not have, is needed to describe what “time” means at the Planck scale.

Whether time is continuous or discrete, whether it had a beginning, whether it will have an end, these are questions our physics cannot currently answer.

IV. The Experience of Time. Phenomenology

Between Augustine’s psychological time and physics’ geometrical time, there is a third perspective: the phenomenology of temporal experience.

Husserl’s time-consciousness:

Edmund Husserl, Heidegger’s teacher, analyzed the structure of the “living present” in On the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time (1928).

The present moment, for Husserl, is not a knife-edge, an instantaneous now with no duration.

It is a specious present, a small stretch of time that is experienced as simultaneous.

Within this living present:

retention, the just-past, still held in the present experience, and protention, the about-to-come, already anticipated.

When you hear a melody, you hear the notes as a sequence, not as isolated sounds.

You hear them as a melody because the earlier notes are retained while the later notes are heard.

The present moment of hearing contains, within it, the retained past and the anticipated future.

This is why music is possible. This is why speech is possible.

Without retention and protention, each moment would be completely isolated, no connection to what came before, no anticipation of what comes next.

(This is why I cannot listen to music as background noise. The melody requires the whole present. You cannot half-hear it.)

Time-consciousness makes experience coherent.

The phenomenology of boredom:

Heidegger, in his 1929-30 lecture course The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics, analyzes boredom as a fundamental mood that reveals the structure of time.

When bored, time slows. Conspicuously.

You become aware of time’s passing precisely because it is not passing.

The structure revealed: time is normally transparent. We live through it without noticing it, absorbed in our activities.

Boredom makes time opaque, suddenly visible, heavy, resistant.

The bored person is held by time, unable to fill it, unable to move through it, exposed to its pure passing.

This is why boredom is so uncomfortable. It exposes the temporality of existence that absorption normally conceals.

The phenomenology of flow:

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi’s concept of flow, the state of complete absorption in a challenging activity, is the opposite of boredom.

In flow: time disappears. The person is entirely in the present, no past, no future, no awareness of duration.

Athletes, musicians, programmers, writers in the state of deep work, all report the disappearance of time.

Two hours pass in what feels like twenty minutes. Or twenty minutes feel like two hours.

The experience of time’s duration is not measured by the clock. It is constituted by the quality of attention.

Full attention: time disappears. Empty attention: time expands unbearably.

V. Memory. The Past That Lives

Augustine said: the present of past things is memory.

Memory is not a recording. It is a reconstruction.

The reconstructive nature of memory:

Every time you remember something, you reconstruct it, from fragments, from expectations, from your current emotional state, from the story you have been telling about your own past.

The remembered past is not the actual past. It is a present construction of what the past was.

This is not a failure of memory. It is what memory is.

The past, as experienced in memory, is always filtered through the present self doing the remembering.

Proust:

Marcel Proust spent 3,000 pages (I read them,yeah!) exploring this in In Search of Lost Time, the madeleine dipped in tea that suddenly releases a memory not as a record but as a full sensory re-experience, involuntary memory, the past that comes unbidden, more vivid than voluntary recollection, and the narrator’s realization that what he was searching for, lost time, could only be recovered in art, which makes the past permanent by making it the present of the reader. (Wooohoooo, this is Filiz’s longest sentence, a revenge of time spent reading Proust! :))

“The true paradises are the paradises we have lost.”

(3,000 pages on this one idea. And every page earns its place. This is either the most self-indulgent novel ever written or the most honest one. Probably both.)

The physics of memory:

Memory is encoded in synaptic connections, in the physical structure of the brain.

When you remember, neurons fire in patterns that recreate the original pattern.

But: each time you remember, the memory is slightly altered, reconsolidated with new information.

The memory of a memory is not the original experience. It is the memory of the last time you remembered it.

(Which means the memories I am most certain of are probably the most altered. Comforting thought.)

The past, neurologically, is continuously rewritten in the present.

VI. The Future. Expectation and Anxiety

Augustine: the present of future things is expectation.

The future does not exist. And yet we live oriented toward it.

Every action is directed toward a future state. Every plan assumes a future. Every hope, every fear, every intention, all are directed toward what is not yet.

Heidegger’s Entwurf, projection, the way Dasein always throws itself ahead toward possibilities.

We are not beings who have a future. We are beings who are always already projecting ourselves toward a future, who exist in the mode of the not-yet.

The tyranny of the future:

The future that concerns us most is the one we cannot plan for: death.

The awareness of mortality, explicit or implicit, shapes the entire temporal horizon of experience.

Everything is done in the light of finitude.

Every choice involves the other choices that are thereby not made.

Every moment contains the mortality that makes it this moment and not an infinite succession of others.

This is not morbidity. It is the condition of seriousness.

The person who genuinely lives in the awareness of finitude takes their time seriously, knows that this moment is not replaceable, that this conversation, this decision, this experience, will not come again.

The person who lives in denial of finitude can always defer. There will be time later, another chance, a tomorrow that is structurally identical to today.

Death cancels the infinite deferral. It makes the present the only time there is.

VII. The Eternal Present

Against the rushing of time, the Buddhist, the Stoic, the contemplative traditions of many cultures have proposed a different relationship with time:

The eternal present.

Not eternity as infinite duration, time going on forever.

But eternity as the depth of the present, the present moment experienced in its fullness, without the pull of past or future.

Marcus Aurelius:

“Confine yourself to the present.”

Not as a counsel of forgetfulness, but as a recognition that the past and future are not available to us. Only the present is real. Only the present can be inhabited.

The mind that is always elsewhere, in the regretted past, in the anxious future, is never where it is.

The physics of the present:

In special relativity, the light cone of an event divides spacetime into three regions: the past (what could have caused this event), the future (what this event could cause), and the spacelike-separated region, a vast set of events that cannot be causally connected to this event at all.

The “absolute present” in this sense is not a thin slice. It is enormous.

The contemplative idea of a deep, full present is philosophically interesting. But it does not map onto the physics in any tidy way.

The poetry is tempting. The physics does not cooperate.

VIII. Time and Language

Wittgenstein noted: the grammar of our language generates philosophical puzzles about time.

“Time passes,” but what is the subject? What is doing the passing?

“The same moment,” what makes moments the same or different?

“Now,” the most indexical word in language, pointing to the present, cannot be given a description that is not itself indexical.

Every attempt to describe “now” uses another word that refers to now.

The grammar of temporal language is not a description of time. It is a form of life, a set of practices for coordinating human activity in time.

When we ask “what is time?” we may be asking: what is the grammar of temporal language?

And the answer may be: there is no deeper answer. The grammar is what it is. The practices are what they are.

Time is what we do with it!

IX. What We Don’t Know

After Augustine, after Heidegger, after Einstein, after quantum mechanics, what do we know about time?

We know:

Time dilates with velocity and gravity.

The arrow of time is associated with entropy increase, though why entropy was low at the Big Bang remains unexplained.

Time had a beginning, the Big Bang.

Below the Planck time, time has no meaning.

We don’t know:

Whether time flows or is static.

Whether the present is real or relative.

Whether time is continuous or discrete.

Whether time had a beginning in any absolute sense.

What happened before the Big Bang, or whether “before” applies.

Why the universe began in a low-entropy state, which is the real origin of the arrow of time.

Whether time is fundamental or emergent.

The deepest mystery:

Why does time seem to flow?

In the block universe, all moments equally exist. Nothing moves. Nothing passes. The universe is a static four-dimensional structure.

And yet: you experience time as flowing.

The present feels different from the past. The future feels open in a way the past does not.

Why?

This question, the question of why we experience time as flowing in a world where physics suggests nothing flows, is the hardest question in the philosophy of time.

It connects physics to consciousness. It connects the structure of the world to the structure of experience.

It has no agreed answer.

X. Living in Time

All of this philosophy, all of this physics, and time remains what it was before any of it:

The medium of your life. The stuff you are made of. The dimension in which everything happens, everything you remember, everything you anticipate, everything you are doing right now.

Augustine’s restless heart. Heidegger’s being-toward-death. Einstein’s dilating clocks. Proust’s involuntary memory. The Stoic’s present moment.

All of these are attempts to understand the same thing:

What it is to be a being who exists in time, who is constituted by past, oriented toward future, and always already in the present that passes before it can be held.

The answer is not available. The question is indispensable.

“Si nemo ex me quaerat, scio.”

If no one asks me, I know.

I know it right now, this moment, this passing, this movement from what was to what will be through the knife-edge of what is.

I know it in the way I know how to breathe.

And when I try to explain it, I do not know.

Further reading:

Augustine. Confessions (397). (trans. Henry Chadwick, Oxford World’s Classics). Book XI for the philosophy of time.

Heidegger. Being and Time (1927). (trans. Macquarrie & Robinson, or Stambaugh). Division Two for temporality and death.

Husserl. On the Phenomenology of the Consciousness of Internal Time (1928). (trans. Brough, Kluwer).

McTaggart. “The Unreality of Time” (1908). Mind 17, 457. The A-series / B-series distinction; essential.

Price. Time’s Arrow and Archimedes’ Point (1996). Oxford University Press.

Barbour. The End of Time (1999). Oxford University Press.

Rovelli. The Order of Time (2018).

Proust. In Search of Lost Time :)) (Filizko suffered, now it is your turn! Ahahah!) :)) (trans. Moncrieff & Kilmartin).

Penrose. The Road to Reality (2004). Chapters 27-28 for time asymmetry.
entry.summary: The most intimate and most mysterious of all phenomena. We live inside it. We cannot step outside it to examine it. And the closer we look, the stranger it becomes.

entry.title: Erotapokriseis XI
entry.content:
EN:

Helloggg my dear readers,

One of the sweetest surprises of keeping this blog has been discovering the questions that come back to me from the other side of the screen. I’ve answered most of your messages, but I wanted to save a few of them here, in this little archive of conversations.

TR:

Sevgili okurlarım,

Bu blogu yazmanın en tatlı sürprizlerinden biri, ekranın öbür tarafından bana dönen sorular oldu her zaman! İyi ki varsınız! Mesajlarınızın çoğuna cevap verdim, ama bazılarını bu küçük sohbet arşivinde saklamak istedim. :)

1) Q: Why does the renormalization group feel less like a technique in physics and more like a way of thinking? renormalization group

A: Because it isn’t a tool you reach for; it’s a lens you can’t put down. A technique answers one question. RG tells you which questions even survive once you step back far enough to see the shape of a thing. After a while you start asking it of everything, not just physics: what stays true when I stop looking so closely? That is not a method. That is a way of seeing.

2) Q: When the scale of something changes, does its truth change as well?

A: The parameters do. The electric charge you measure literally depends on how closely you look. What changes, though, is not the truth itself but which description is the honest one at that scale. The world isn’t lying to you at low resolution. It’s telling you a coarser truth, and RG is the grammar that connects the coarse one to the fine one.

3) Q: Does RG suggest that the world is understood not through details themselves, but through the way details are forgotten?

A: Yes, and that’s the part that gives me chills. RG makes forgetting rigorous: it tells you exactly which details you are allowed to throw away, and then proves the answer doesn’t depend on them. We spend our lives thinking knowledge means holding on to more. RG says the deepest understanding is knowing precisely what to let go of!

4) Q: Why does the idea of universality affect you so much: because order emerges from chaos, or because different systems seem to speak the same language?

A: The second, and it isn’t close. Order from chaos is beautiful, but I’ve made my peace with it. What undoes me is that a lump of iron and a jar of fluid near their critical points obey the exact same numbers, having never met, sharing none of the details. What they do share is the deep grammar: the same symmetry, the same dimension, the same short reach of interaction. It’s the universe rhyming with itself, and the rhyme has a reason, which somehow makes it more chilling, not less. Universality is the closest physics comes to admitting reality has only a few real ideas and endless disguises. I will write a blog post on Chaos very soon! Tbh, you inspired me to write one! Cheers. :)

5) Q: If physics tells us that the same explanation does not hold at every scale, could that also be true of human life?

A: We stopped demanding a single explanation for every scale; we use quarks for one regime and fluids for another, and nobody calls that failure… I think, I need to think about this one a little more.

I will answer this later. Sorry! Thanks for the question!

6) Q: What fascinates you most about quantum error correction?

A: I’m still a beginner in this field. Learning, and not understanding enough yet for fascination!

7) Q: When we try to protect a quantum computer, what are we really protecting: computation, information, or possibility?

A: All three, but most fundamentally, information.

Computation is what we want to do with it; possibility is the strange quantum form it takes before measurement. But what we are really protecting is fragile information from leaking into the world too soon.

A quantum computer is powerful because it can hold possibilities coherently. Error correction is our way of saying: not yet, universe. Do not turn this into history before the computation is done. :)

8) Q: Is decoherence only a physical problem, or can it also be seen as the universe’s resistance to preserving memory?

A: Physically, decoherence is not the universe “resisting” anything; it is the environment entangling with the system and carrying information about it away.

But romanticizing is free, right? :) So, poetically: yes. It feels like the universe reminding us that memory is not free, and that every preserved possibility has to be protected from a world constantly trying to read it. Cheers!

This is almost the same question as Q1, asked by two different people. I tried to answer it the way the reader asked:

9) Q: Why does the renormalization group feel less like a physics technique and more like a worldview?

A: Because the renormalization group teaches you that not every detail deserves to survive a change of scale.

Some things are relevant, some are irrelevant, and some only look important because you are standing too close. That feels less like a technical lesson in physics and more like a way of thinking about almost everything: ideas, people, pain, memory, even the self.

What remains true after you zoom out? That is the question. :)

entry.title: The Renormalization Group: The Deepest Idea in Physics

link.title: The Renormalization Group: The Deepest Idea in Physics

entry.content:
There is an idea in physics that is so deep that once you understand it, you cannot unsee it!

It is everywhere…

In the flow of a turbulent river. In the behavior of magnets near the critical point. In the reason quantum field theory works at all. In the structure of the Standard Model. In the hierarchy of scales in nature.

The idea is the renormalization group.

It is not a group in the mathematical sense. It does not have inverses. It is not a renormalization in the original sense. It is not about removing infinities.

It is a way of thinking about how physics changes with scale, how the description of a system transforms as you zoom in or zoom out, and what remains invariant under this transformation.

It is, I will argue, the deepest idea in physics.

I. The Problem of Scale

Physics has a problem.

At every scale of nature, there is structure.

At \(10^{-35}\) m: quantum gravity, Planck scale. At \(10^{-18}\) m: quarks, gluons, electroweak unification. At \(10^{-15}\) m: protons, neutrons, nuclear physics. At \(10^{-10}\) m: atoms, atomic physics. At \(10^{-9}\) m: molecules, chemistry. At \(10^{-6}\) m: cells, biology. At \(10^{0}\) m: human scale, classical mechanics. At \(10^{21}\) m: galaxies, galactic dynamics. At \(10^{26}\) m: the observable universe, cosmology.

Sixty orders of magnitude of structure.

The miracle: you do not need to know all scales to describe physics at any given scale.

To describe the motion of a billiard ball, you do not need to know the positions of all its atoms.

To describe atomic physics, you do not need to know the internal structure of the nucleus.

To describe nuclear physics, you do not need to know the details of quark confinement.

Physics at each scale is largely autonomous, decoupled from the details of smaller scales.

Why?

The renormalization group explains why.

II. Wilson’s Revolutionary Idea

Kenneth Wilson (Nobel Prize 1982) transformed our understanding of quantum field theory and statistical mechanics in the early 1970s.

His key insight:

The physics at long wavelengths (low energies) is determined by an effective theory, obtained by integrating out the short-wavelength (high-energy) degrees of freedom.

This is Wilsonian renormalization.

Consider a system of spins on a lattice, a ferromagnet. Lattice spacing: \(a\). Total size: \(L\).

The degrees of freedom: spins \(s_i\) at each lattice site.

Wilson’s procedure, block spin renormalization:

  1. Coarse-grain: average spins in blocks of size \(ba\) (\(b > 1\), typically \(b = 2\)).

  2. Rescale: redefine the length unit: \(x o x/b\) so the new lattice has the same spacing \(a\).

  3. Renormalize fields: rescale the block spin to restore canonical normalization.

The result: a new effective theory with the same form as the original, but with renormalized coupling constants.

The couplings flow: \(g o g'(g, b)\)

This is the renormalization group transformation: \(\mathcal{R}_b: \{g\} o \{g'\}\)

It forms a semigroup. Composition works, but there are no inverses (you cannot un-coarse-grain).

III. Fixed Points and Universality

Under repeated RG transformations, the coupling constants flow in theory space.

The flow has special points:

Fixed points:

\[\mathcal{R}_b: g^* o g^*\]

At a fixed point, the physics is scale-invariant. It looks the same at all scales.

There are two types:

UV fixed point (ultraviolet): The theory flows toward this point as you zoom in (to shorter distances). The theory at the UV fixed point describes the fundamental short-distance physics.

IR fixed point (infrared): The theory flows toward this point as you zoom out (to longer distances). The theory at the IR fixed point describes the long-distance, low-energy behavior.

The Gaussian fixed point: The free field theory, no interactions. Many theories flow to this in the IR. This is why perturbation theory works: near the Gaussian fixed point, interactions are small.

Relevant, marginal, and irrelevant operators:

Near a fixed point, perturb the theory by an operator \(\mathcal{O}_i\) with coupling \(g_i\):

Under RG: \(g_i o b^{y_i} g_i\)

  • \(y_i > 0\): relevant, coupling grows under RG. Becomes important at long distances.
  • \(y_i = 0\): marginal, coupling unchanged (at linear order). Need higher-order analysis.
  • \(y_i < 0\): irrelevant, coupling shrinks under RG. Becomes unimportant at long distances.

Universality:

Near an IR fixed point, only relevant operators matter. Irrelevant operators vanish.

This explains universality: why different microscopic systems show identical large-scale behavior.

Different systems with different microscopic details flow to the same IR fixed point.

The Ising model, the liquid-gas transition, certain polymer systems, all belong to the same universality class.

Their critical exponents are identical: \( u = 0.6301..., \quad \eta = 0.0364..., \quad eta = 0.3265...\)

Not approximately identical. Identical to many decimal places.

Why? Because near the critical point, only a handful of relevant operators matter. The microscopic details are irrelevant in the technical RG sense.

The universality class is determined by the symmetry and dimensionality, not by the atomic details.

IV. Critical Phenomena and Scaling

At the critical point, the fixed point of the RG, the system is scale-invariant.

This produces power law behavior:

\[\xi \sim \lvert T - T_c vert^{- u}\]

The correlation length \(\xi\) diverges as \(T o T_c\).

All other thermodynamic quantities exhibit power laws near \(T_c\):

\[m \sim \lvert T - T_c vert^{ eta} \quad ext{(magnetization)}\] \[\chi \sim \lvert T - T_c vert^{-\gamma} \quad ext{(susceptibility)}\] \[C \sim \lvert T - T_c vert^{-\alpha} \quad ext{(specific heat)}\]

The critical exponents \( u, eta, \gamma, \alpha, \delta, \eta\) are universal: same for all systems in the universality class.

They satisfy scaling relations:

\(\alpha + 2 eta + \gamma = 2 \quad ext{(Rushbrooke)}\) \(\gamma = u(2 - \eta) \quad ext{(Fisher)}\) \( u d = 2 - \alpha \quad ext{(hyperscaling)}\)

These relations are not empirical. They follow from RG scaling, from the assumption of a fixed point.

Wilson computed the critical exponents using the \(\epsilon\)-expansion: expand around \(d = 4 - \epsilon\) dimensions, compute perturbatively in \(\epsilon\), set \(\epsilon = 1\) for \(d = 3\).

The results agreed with experiments to extraordinary precision.

For the first time, the universal critical exponents were computed from first principles.

V. The RG in Quantum Field Theory

In QFT, the renormalization group takes a different but equivalent form.

The Callan-Symanzik equation:

Physical observables are independent of the arbitrary renormalization scale \(\mu\).

\[\mu rac{d}{d\mu} \mathcal{G}^{(n)} = 0\]

This gives:

\[\left[\mu rac{\partial}{\partial\mu} + eta(g) rac{\partial}{\partial g} - n\gamma(g) ight]\mathcal{G}^{(n)} = 0\]

The beta function \( eta(g)\):

\[ eta(g) = \mu rac{dg}{d\mu}\]

describes how the coupling constant changes with the renormalization scale.

  • \( eta(g) > 0\): coupling increases with energy (IR free, UV divergent)
  • \( eta(g) < 0\): coupling decreases with energy (asymptotic freedom)
  • \( eta(g^*) = 0\): fixed point

Asymptotic freedom:

In QCD (the theory of strong interactions), the beta function is:

\[ eta(g_s) = - rac{g_s^3}{16\pi^2} \left( rac{11}{3}N_c - rac{2}{3}N_f ight)\]

For \(N_c = 3\) colors, \(N_f = 6\) flavors:

\[ eta(g_s) = - rac{7g_s^3}{16\pi^2} < 0\]

The strong coupling decreases at high energies.

At short distances (high energies): quarks are free. At long distances (low energies): quarks are confined.

This is asymptotic freedom, discovered by Gross, Politzer, and Wilczek in 1973 (Nobel Prize 2004).

It explains why perturbation theory works at high energies for QCD but not at low energies: the coupling is small at high energies, large at low energies.

The running of the coupling:

\[\alpha_s(\mu) = rac{\alpha_s(\mu_0)} {1 + rac{\alpha_s(\mu_0)}{2\pi} \left( rac{11}{3}N_c - rac{2}{3}N_f ight) \ln(\mu/\mu_0)}\]

At \(\mu = M_Z = 91.2\) GeV: \(\alpha_s \approx 0.118\) At \(\mu = 1\) GeV: \(\alpha_s \approx 0.5\)

The same coupling, running with scale.

VI. The Effective Field Theory Program

Wilson’s RG framework provides the conceptual foundation for effective field theory (EFT), the most powerful tool in modern physics.

The idea:

At any given energy scale \(E\), physics is described by an effective Lagrangian containing all operators consistent with the symmetries, organized by their dimension:

\[\mathcal{L}_{eff} = \sum_i rac{c_i}{\Lambda^{d_i - 4}}\mathcal{O}_i\]

where \(\Lambda\) is the cutoff scale, \(d_i\) is the dimension of operator \(\mathcal{O}_i\), and \(c_i\) are Wilson coefficients.

Operators with \(d_i > 4\) are suppressed by powers of \(E/\Lambda\).

At energies \(E \ll \Lambda\): only \(d \leq 4\) operators matter. The EFT is renormalizable.

At energies \(E \sim \Lambda\): higher-dimension operators become important. New physics appears.

The Standard Model as an EFT:

The Standard Model, which we thought was a fundamental theory, is an effective field theory.

It is valid at energies below some cutoff \(\Lambda_{NP}\), the scale of new physics.

The fact that the SM is renormalizable, contains only \(d \leq 4\) operators, is not a fundamental requirement.

It is an automatic consequence of the EFT framework: at low energies, higher-dimension operators decouple.

The SM is not fundamental. It is the IR description of some UV theory we have not yet found.

Gravity as an EFT:

Even General Relativity can be treated as an EFT, expanded in powers of \(E/m_P\):

\[\mathcal{L}_{gravity} = rac{m_P^2}{2}R + c_1 R^2 + c_2 R_{\mu u}R^{\mu u} + rac{c_3}{m_P^2}R^3 + ...\]

At energies \(E \ll m_P\): only the Einstein-Hilbert term matters. GR is a valid effective theory.

At energies \(E \sim m_P\): all higher-order terms matter. Quantum gravity is necessary.

This is why we can do reliable calculations in quantum gravity at low energies: GR as an EFT gives well-defined predictions, without needing a complete theory of quantum gravity.

VII. The Hierarchy Problem. Where RG Hurts

The renormalization group also reveals one of the deepest problems in physics.

The Higgs mass problem:

The Higgs boson mass receives quantum corrections:

\[m_H^2 = (m_H^{bare})^2 + \delta m_H^2\]

where:

\[\delta m_H^2 \sim rac{3\Lambda^2}{8\pi^2 v^2} \left(m_t^2 - rac{m_W^2}{2} - rac{m_Z^2}{4} - rac{m_H^2}{4} ight)\]

The correction scales as \(\Lambda^2\), quadratically with the UV cutoff.

If \(\Lambda = m_P \approx 10^{19}\) GeV:

\[\delta m_H^2 \sim \left( rac{10^{19}}{125} ight)^2 m_H^2 \sim 10^{34} m_H^2\]

The bare mass must cancel this to 34 decimal places to give the observed Higgs mass of 125 GeV.

This is the hierarchy problem, or the naturalness problem.

The Higgs mass is quadratically sensitive to UV physics. To get a light Higgs at 125 GeV, the bare parameters must be fine-tuned to extraordinary precision.

Fine-tuning of this magnitude seems unnatural. It suggests we are missing something.

Proposed solutions:

Supersymmetry: Fermion loops cancel boson loops. The quadratic divergence cancels:

\[\delta m_H^2|_{SUSY} \sim m_{SUSY}^2 \ln(\Lambda/m_{SUSY})\]

Logarithmic instead of quadratic. Natural if \(m_{SUSY} \sim ext{TeV}\).

LHC found no SUSY at the TeV scale. Either SUSY is at higher mass, less natural, or SUSY does not solve the hierarchy problem.

Compositeness / Little Higgs: The Higgs is a composite particle, a pseudo-Goldstone boson, at a scale \(\sim 1\) TeV. The quadratic divergence is cut off at the compositeness scale.

No evidence found at LHC.

Extra dimensions: The Planck scale in 4D is large because gravity spreads into extra dimensions. The true Planck scale is \(\sim\) TeV. No hierarchy.

No evidence found.

Anthropic selection: The Higgs mass is fine-tuned because only in universes with light Higgs bosons does complex chemistry, and life, exist.

We cannot falsify this. Many physicists find it unsatisfying.

The RG perspective on naturalness:

The hierarchy problem is a statement about the RG flow.

The Higgs mass operator is relevant at the UV scale: it grows as you flow to lower energies. To keep it small in the IR, you need precise cancellations in the UV.

A natural theory is one where all IR parameters are determined by UV parameters without fine-tuning, where the relevant operators are either absent or protected by symmetry.

The Standard Model is not natural in this sense.

This is not merely aesthetic. It is a strong hint that the SM is incomplete, that new physics exists at some scale that protects the Higgs mass.

We have not found it.

VIII. The Deep Message

The renormalization group tells us something profound about the structure of reality.

Reality is organized by scale.

At each scale, there is an effective description: a set of relevant degrees of freedom and their interactions.

The description at each scale is largely autonomous, insensitive to the details of shorter scales.

This is why science is possible.

If physics at the human scale depended sensitively on the positions of every quark in every proton, if there were no decoupling of scales, no effective theory would exist at any scale.

Everything would depend on everything else. No prediction would be possible. Science would be impossible.

The decoupling of scales, the organization of nature into largely independent effective theories, is the precondition for scientific knowledge.

The RG explains this decoupling.

And it tells us more:

The fundamental theory, whatever UV fixed point the RG flows from, need not be known to do physics at low energies.

The IR physics is determined by the universality class, by the symmetries and the dimensionality, not by the microscopic details.

This is either: (a) a deep truth about reality: nature is organized so that knowledge at each scale does not require knowledge of all scales (b) a feature of the RG mathematical structure: a property of the equations we use to describe nature (c) an anthropic observation: only in a universe with scale decoupling would observers exist to notice it

Probably all three.

IX. Fixed Points Are the Fundamental Objects

I want to make a claim that is not universally shared but that I believe is correct:

The fixed points of the RG, the scale-invariant theories, are the fundamental objects in physics.

Not the specific theories at specific scales. The fixed points.

The Gaussian fixed point: free field theory. The Wilson-Fisher fixed point: critical phenomena. The UV fixed points of asymptotically free theories.

These are the organizing structures around which physics at all scales is organized.

The RG flow connects them: physics flows from UV fixed points (short-distance physics) to IR fixed points (long-distance physics).

The theories we observe at any given scale are points on these flows: transient descriptions, valid over a range of scales, connecting the UV structure to the IR structure.

The fixed points are eternal. The theories between them are approximate.

This is the deepest message of the RG:

Nature is not described by a single theory at a single scale.

It is described by a web of effective theories, organized by their RG flows, anchored at fixed points.

The quest for a “Theory of Everything” is the quest for the UV fixed point: the theory from which all others flow.

We have not found it.

But the RG tells us what we are looking for.
